Mr. Speaker, in rising to make the remarks which I believe it is my duty to make on the present occasion, I wish to say that, at this stage of the debate I intend to be as brief as possible. I do not wish to take up the time of this House in wandering far from the question which we are now called upon to discuss. I shall, therefore, not attempt to discuss many of the questions that have been brought up by members on both sides of this House.
I claim, Mr. Speaker, that the only important questions .before us at the present time are men, munitions, ships, food and the financing of this great war, and, in my opinion, the most important of all is food.
I 'believe this Government should move very carefully and study well the great question of the shortage of food. I feel, after they have weighed the question from all sides, they will come, to the conclusion that the young men should not at this critical time be removed from the farms. It must, however, be clearly understood that the farmers in our part of the country are ready to do their share, either at the front or on the farm, in winning this war, and I dislike hearing the slurring insinuations that are thrown across the floor of this House at Quebec, because nothing but harm can come out of such statements. You cannot produce more food and, at the same time, take the men from the farms. You must choose what you consider the most essential at this time, and then carry out one plan or the other. You must not endeavour to do both with the same class of men. I consider a great deal of time has been lost and a great deal of harm has been done by discouraging the farmers and young men of this country by pulling them from one exemption tribunal to another and not <nv-

ing them any satisfactory answer as to where their best work may be carried on in order to win the great struggle which is now being waged. If those young men are wrongly directed by this Government, the ministers of the Crown and hon. members supporting the Government will be held by the people of this country to be responsible, for the action they have taken and the method they ha/ve used in carrying out what I consider an unnecessary law. They say that we can replace those farmers by sending out men from the cities. It is absurd to think that anything of the kind can be done. How, many men can you get out in the morning and milk ten cows and do the same thing at night? If they were willing, not more than one out of ten can milk, and not more than one out of twenty is willing. And when you stop the dairy industry of this country, you stop the production of cheese, which is a most essential and necessary food for the soldiers at the front.
What advice do we get from our food controllers, both in Canada and in Great Britain? Are we carrying out their views by taking men from the farms? Let us see what they say. Although this has already been placed on Hansard, I feel it is of such great importance that it cannot be too carefully considered. We even have the statement of the Prime Minister of Canada that food may be the winning card in this war. We also have the opinion of Lord Rhondda, the British food controller, who, from London on the 10th of April, cabled the Cam ada Food Board as follows:
In these stern days it is inspiring to learn that Canada is tackling the food problem with redoubled energy. The terrific pressure on our military front makes it all the more imperative that those behind the lines should strain every nerve to defeat the enemy's avowed object of destroying the British Empire. Germany hoped first to starve the Old Country by the submarine campaign and then to smash her land forces. She has failed to starve us and she will fail to smash us hut we cannot achieve victory without food. There never was a time when it was more needed. The Canadian farmer and the Canadian farm hand now have the opportunity to make an effective reply to the enemy's present onslaughts by bending their undivided energies to the increased production of those food supplies for which we depend to such vital extent on your great Dominion.
We also have our own Doctor Robertson, who has .assured us that the world faces a food situation that is nothing short of appalling.
The increased dependence of our Allies, France, Italy and: Belgium, upon ns for food production is shown by the following
facts: In France the average yearly production of wheat for the five years preceding the war was 317,000,000 bushels. In 1916, the production had fallen to no less than 214,000,000 bushels, and in 1917 the crop was estimated at 161,000,000 bushels. Likewise in Italy, the average pre-war production for five years amounted to 183,000,000 bushels. In 1910 this had dropped to
176.000.	000 bushels, and in 1917 the estimate was 147,000,000 bushels. In Belgium the average pre-war production was almost 15,000,000 bushels. It fell in 1916 to almost
12.000.	000 bushels. The estimate for 1917 only amounted to* 9,000,000 bushels. The total reduction in those three countries amounted to over 198,000,000 bushels, representing >a reduction from pre-war production of nearly thirty-eight per cent. In view of these facts Canada finds itself one of the most important factors, if not the most important factor, in the food situation. Supplies from Eastern Europe no longer exist. Supplies from Australia and Africa are too fiar away to be moved. As Lord Rhondda has said: What we ask from the United States and Canada we cannot procure elsewhere. As between ourselves and the United States we have a far larger exportable surplus of wheat than she has. In the past year our exportable wheat surplus amounted to 154,000,000 bushels, while the United) States had only one-third1 of that amount. Canada is called upon to be a factor in saving the world which is face to face with starvation. Now, Mr. Speaker, you can see by this shortage that Canada and the United States are looked upon to save the situation. We have, in our great West, vast prairies and wheat land which can produce an immense quantity of all kinds of grain, if we can only get the help to cultivate those vast fields. We also have, in our own country, a large quantity of land not cultivated on account of shortage of labour, and if the Government takes away many of our hoys, the situation will be still more serious.
The Government must be congratulated on the stand they have taken in removing the duty on tractors to assist in greater production. Should that increase production, as I am ready to admit it will, would it not have been wise, under the same Order in Council, to go further and .absolutely eliminate all the duty from farm implements? No doubt there would have been some objections from manufacturers, but the Government could have called the measure a war-time measure and waved the old flag, and it might have passed with-

out any .serious objections being raised. Some years ago there were brought uip in this House cases where manufacturers sold farm implements to dealers in the United States, paying the duty, and those dealers sold them back again to our western farmers, another duty being paid, and even then those implements were sold1 for less money than the price at which our dealers could sell them. Does any hon. member think that those manufacturers still require protection on the part of the .Government? This is an opportune time, when the war is on, to remove the duty on farm implements altogether.
A pledge was made by members of this Government to the farmers of my county that the latter would not be taken from their farms., that the object of the compulsory service legislation was to get at the slackers in large cities, such as Montreal. The same statement was made by some clergymen on public platforms, and no doubt they had authority to -make such statements. If not, they should have had authority before making such statements on public platforms. I believe the Government should be in a position to tell the farmers what they really intend to do. They should settle down to some kind of a policy whereby the people of this country will know what they have to do, and in that way the Government will prevent all this trouble that is now going on. They should call off many of the officers who are, without any reason, arresting young men. Judgment should be used, and when a young man is ready and willing to go he should not be taken as a criminal and locked up. All he asks is to be notified when he is wanted and where he has to report.
In my constituency, on the 16th of April, two young men were arrested; they were marched four miles down the track that evening and placed in jail. Two other young men, one only nineteen years of age, were asked to come to a village, and when they drove up with a team they were taken away from the team, not being allowed to drive the team home again, and put into jail. The next morning a man was taken from a field where he was working and also put into jail. He was not allowed even to go home and change his clothes. The men who were put into jail in the evening were taken out in the morning and given breakfast, and then they did not receive anything more to eat until night. They went without dinner. They had no chairs to sit down on, and there were no sanitary ar-

rangements. They were locked up in one room, being treated worse than criminals. At night they were given supper and were again locked up. The Government should see that the proper men are authorized to bring these men wherever they want them. Everybody is willing to help to win the war, but what the young men want is to know when they are wanted and where they have to report. A letter with a three cent stamp on it would have brought any one of those young men wherever they were required to report. They were later on taken out of jail, and four or five officers took them to Sherbrooke or Quebec. It is no wonder riots occur, in Quebec when young men are treated that way. It must have cost twenty or twenty-five dollars to round up each of these men. I did not intend to bring this matter up; but I have received letters from many of my electors requesting that this should he discussed in the House of Commons, and I hope nothing of the kind will happen again.

Mr. Speaker, this debate has already continued to such a considerable length that it is not my desire to prolong it unduly; but a consideration of the Budget touches upon the national interests at so many points that I believe it provides a suitable opportunity for the discussion of national affairs as would be provided under possibly no other circumstances. While, Sir, it gives occasion for constructive criticism, and also perhaps criticism of the opposite kind, I may say that I do not propose to approach the questions which I shall briefly discuss from the point of view of party politics at all. I believe that to-day the people of this country are not particularly concerned with party polities. They are interested in the war. They are interested in the heavy financial responsibilities that they have to bear, and in all those *things which result from the conduct of the war.
The national interests are to-day already iso delicately balanced that it would be nothing short of criminal on the part of the members of this House to attempt to make this the occasion for the making of party capital or for the securing of any purely party advantage. We have arrived a^ the most critical stage of the war. Our financial responsibilities are extremely heavy, [DOT]and the harmony which ought to exist, but which, unfortunately, does not exist amongst the members of the various races which go to make up this Dominion, deserves, to my mind, a different treatment

from that which was accorded to it yesterday on the occasion of the speech delivered by the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken).
It is true that nearly all of us on this side of the (House differed and still differ from hon. gentlemen opposite on the question of conscription. It is not my intention or desire to re-thrash old straw. We were and are honestly opposed to conscription, and I believe we are right. I believe further that the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) showed the only . statesmanlike course we should have pursued in that matter. Now the Act has been tried out, and since we have heard hon. members of the Government admitting it has been a failure and have amended the Act within the last two weeks, I think I am absolutely correct in saying the leader of the Opposition will not be required to await the verdict of history, but that he is vindicated already in the opinion of the majority of the people of this Dominion. While we cannot support the Government in all its measures-I think every member on this side should realize and does realize he has nevertheless a responsibility to his constituents, and that it is his duty to support whatever legislation may be brought down by the Union Government which is deserving of support. It is no less the duty of hon. members on this side of the House to offer suggestions and criticism, constructive wherever possible, and to do all they can to advance the interests of the people of this Dominion.
Those of us who are new members have observed the proceedings of this House with a great deal of interest, and particularly with a view to observing how the Union Government will reconcile in a practical way its protestations of democracy with the actions of the executive branch of Parliament, so far as it relates to the members of the House at large. I admit, as a new member, that we have a great deal to learn but after all the new members come here with certain very well defined convictions. Among these, first of all, is the duty we owe to our constituents; we must not forget that we should represent their views. Secondly, we have the conviction, just as strong, that the Cabinet owes a direct responsibility to and derives its powers from the members of this House, and through them, from the people of this country. Believing that, I have observed, if not with surprise, at least with considerable disquiet, the undoubted tendency of the Government to arrogate to themselves powers that I believe should never be surrendered by the members of the House of Commons. We have to-day, as has been stated by the right hon. leader of the Opposition, Government by Order in Council. I do not profess to have any great knowledge of constitutional history or practice, but I have always had the impression that the Cabinet of a democratic country was supposed to employ itself more in the way of administration, and that the legislative function belonged to the House of Commons, directly representing the people. I believe I am right when I say that to-day, to a grave degree, the Cabinet has usurped the legislative functions which ought to rest entirely with the House of Commons. While I should like to enlarge on that point, time does not permit, and I will pass on to the. Budget itself.
It had been my intention if the. Acting Minister of Finance were here, to congratulate him on the very clear and comprehensive address he made in presenting the Budget. But after hearing the speech of (he hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. (Lemieux) I hesitate to do so, because he stated that the speech of the Acting Minister of Finance was really the speech of the Minister (Sir Thomas White). If that be true, I fear it will be a matter of considerable grief to the hon. member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) who told the House 'that it was the best Budget speech he had ever heard. (If the speech was really the brain-child of the Minister of Finance, it would be " the most unkindest cut of all " for the hon. member for Victoria thus to compliment that best beloved friend of his, Sir Thomas White. However that may be, I am inclined to give credit to whom it is apparently due. The Acting Minister of Finance has the honour of pra enting what I think is the largest Budget ever presented in the Dominion of Canada. It is a billion dollar Budget. Four years ago, a Budget of this size would have been thought not only absolutely impossible, hut entirely ruinous to the Dominion. To-day we are spending millions where formerly we were spending perhaps thousands, and conditions are such that we must go on. But I trust that in raising the money that is required we, the representatives of the people of Canada, will not ignore entirely the principle of financial conservation. To-day Canada is prosperous, and she is prosperous because we are living on borrowed money, and because of the abnormal conditions resulting from the war. But the reckoning will come, and with that in mind I am sure it will not he considered unpatriotic to be practical, or
Hear, hear.

-and it is quite unnecessary to place any further burdens upon him to make him realize that to the full. He added insult to injury by stating that this policy would make better citizens of its victims, which is a good deal like the German boast that it will make better citizens of the Belgians to place them under the yoke of German "kultur."
To this school of thinkers we shall say -that on this side we are well able to tell them what we think of them, and I can assure you, Sir, that our opinion of them is a hundred times worse than their opinion of us. But we keejj ourselves under control for the sake of harmony and unity. We understand in a practical and patriotic way that we are at war. To the others-and they are tlhe -majority-we are glad to say that, through their behaviour and their evident disgust of these intolerant and ill-natured attacks, we foresee the near return of the bonne entente, the harmony, union and prosperity which will make of this Canada of ours a better place to live- in, a better place tp thrive in and a better -country to fight for.

and less again do they represent Great Britain. It is the wound which imposes upon us the sacred duty of healing as quickly and as energetically as we can, but, Sir, it is childish to maintain that such a situation, however grave and pitiful it may be, materially changes our general situation, our obligations as a people* at all times, conscious of its honour, its dignity and its liberty.
I love sufficiently my country, Sir, to be moved by the keen desire to see it fulfil its duty to the end, confident as I am that by these means, and this means alone, it will assure for itself the material prosperity which it deserves coupled with the future and the honour of its children. .
Gentlemen, whatever you may say or think, rest assured that alone in the triumph of the Allied Cause will we find the remedy to the evils from which we are now suffering and the guarantee of our future peace and happiness. To attain, Sir, that lofty purpose it is above all others essential, that we should bind together the individual energies of each of us, direct them as a whole towards that supreme object which constitutes the programme of the Prime Minister of Prance, Mr. Briand, a programme unique in the world's history, and which can be summarized in one word "Victory".
Gentlemen, I do not wish a change in the political status of my country ; let it grow and prosper in the future as it has done in the past; let the link that binds us to Britain remain as it is, imaginary in fact but strong in reality. This is all the liberty that I ask for Canada.
Sir, that is the kind of disloyalty I have been preaching in the province of Quebec.
I am proud to say that at a later day in Quebec I preached the same gospel. I am proud ,to say that in speaking in the way which I have indicated I was but following the advice, of my Tight hon. leader. A year later I addressed some young Liberals in Montreal but it is not necessary for me to quote what I said then because my observations on that occasion were along the same lines. The hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken), in concluding his speech yesterday said: "I want the province of Quebec to respect the constitution and to recognize it." I would ask the hon. gentleman if the fact of spreading hatred of one race against another, as he has been doing in the past in his newspaper, is respecting the constitution. We have heard much of late about respecting the constitution but would it not be fair to ask those who are so anxious to have the constitution respected to show some respect for it themselves? I would not like to say anything disagreeable to anybody on the other side of the House, hut if the hon. gentleman to whom I have referred desired to be disagreeable to his own leader he would never have spoken otherwise than he did yesterday, because I contend that since 1911 no one has shown more contempt for
[iMr. Gladti. 1
the constitution than the .right hon. the Prime Minister himself.
Let us have a glimpse at his political career since 1911. There is no use trying to make people believe that we are not respecting the constitution when those who are supposed to have the constitution in their special charge do not themselves respect it. When the Prime Minister was called to office in 1911 his first act was to commit a breach of the constitution. We all know that according to our constitution the members of the Cabinet must foe in accord, that they must all feel and think the same way. Is it necessary to remind the House that the right hon. gentleman, unable to count on a majority elected by the people, was forced to appeal to gentlemen who' had. been elected to combat his Adi-ministration and his policy? In 1916 every body remembers perfectly well that the right hon. gentleman sent a message to the people of Canada in which he stated: " I have promised 500,000 men to England and have promised them without consulting any of my ministers." Would the Kaiser himself dare to do the same even in the autocratic country over which he rules? In 1917, the Prime Minister, after having asked for an extension of the term of Parliament, obtained that extension under the distinct agreement and understanding that no contentions measures would be brought before the House. During the session that followed we had the Canadian Northern, measure which was brought in against the will of the members of this side of the House, aud. which was more than a .contentious measure. It was not exactly a violation of the written law of the country, but it was. a violation o.f the law of honour.
In that same year, 1917, we had another measure brought forward. As I was not in the House at that time, I would like to discuss that question at a certain length, because I think that at an early date it will have to be discussed in this House, and, if not this session, certainly at the next session. I refer to the War-time Elections Act. If there is in our statutes a law which deserves the condemnation of the people of this country and of the members of this House, it is the War-time Elections Act. This Act was passed for what reason? Because w.e were at war? To win the war? No, Sir. The reason that measure was passed in 1917 was that the Government did not dare face public opinion on its own merits, and it had to disfranchise hundreds of thousands of British

citizens who were entitled to vote and who were not favourable to the Government at that time. The worst feature of this legislation, to my mind, especially for those who are always boasting of their loyalty and devotion to the British Empire, is that the Government has adopted measures which are a dishonour to this country and to the British Empire. When men of German and Austrian origin came to this country several years ago, they came, as the Prime Minister stated himself in 1914 and 1915, because they were invited to come here knowing that this was a free country, that their rights would be respected, and that they would be treated as British citizens. They took the oath as British citizens. They knew when they took that oath that they were binding themselves to respect the King, and Constitution of this country. When these men were disfranchised, those who did it simp'y repudiated the King's signature and dishonoured the Crown of England.' They gave that legislation retroactive effect going back ais far as 1902. This is an abuse of a serious character. I intended to quote what the Prime Minister said at that time, but I shall just read two or three lines of it. Speaking of the Germans, in 1914, the horn, gentleman said:
Nearly half a million of the very best citizens of Canada are of German origin, and' I am sure that no one would for one moment desire to utter any word or use any expression in debate which would wound: the self-respect, or hurt the feelings of any of our fellow citizens of German descent.
Some 'hon. MEMBERS:	Hear, hear.

The hon. gentleman added:
We have no reason to doubt, and we do not doubt, that these people will toe absolutely true to the country of their adoption.
Sir, if the Germans in Canada were true to the country of their adoption in 1914 and in 1915, when the Prime Minister spoke of ithemi, they were equally true to- theii adopted country in 1917. But the very reason why the Prime Minister and his colleagues Changed their attitude towards those Germans who were then British citizens was, as I said a moment ago, that they had no fadth whatever in the Government of that time, any more than one-half the' ministers who are now sitting on the other side had faith in the late Government.
In a copy of the Current History Magazine, published by the New York Times a year ago, I found this article:
Germany's Form of Government
Strange to -say I found in this work the very principle of the legislation which was
submitted to the House last session, and which' is called the War-time Elections Act. So that not only wae this legislation not British legislation, and legislation' in which, of course, there is no British fair play, hut it has been borrowed if not stolen from Germany. IThat is a reason, ISir, why that very legislation, especially from the point of view of the ultra loyalists, should be considered a stain on our statutes: and should be expunged from them,. 'Sir, When you think of the way in which the hon. the Prime Minister is trying sometimes to impose his views upon this side of the House, and upon the country, it is very interesting to notice that there is. another man in the world who. uses practically the same language, and here is what he says:
It is a tradition in our House to consider ourselves as designed toy God' to govern the peoples over which it is given us to reign.
Just as. those gentlemen opposite sometimes tell us, we do this because we want to win the war, and we are the only ones who want to win the war.
:My grandfather placed-, hy his own right-
In our case the hon. gentleman cannot, say that he has been placed by the people's right or voice, when he has been placed only by this outrageous and: scandalous legislation, the War-time Elections Act.
