speechtext:
Order. I regret that I
have to call the hon. member to order. It is not competent for him, to speak in disrespectful terms of a,n Act of Parliament, namely, the War-time Elections Act.

Mr. Speaker, I very
willingly abide by your ruling. I do not contend that this legislation is absolutely bad, because it has produced some good results so far. I cannot say that it has produced only bad results, lest . I forget, Sir, that we owe to- it the great privilege, and the greater honour, of retaining .your services as presiding officer of this House. I quote further:
'My grandfather placed, toy his own right, the crown of the kings of Prussia on his head, once more laying stress upon the fact that it was conferred upon him toy the Grace of God alone, not by Parliament, by meetings of the people, or by popular decision'; and that he considered himself as the chosen instrument of Heaven, and as such performed his duties as regent and ruler. Considering myself as the Instrument of the Cord, without heeding the views or opinions of the day, I go my way which is devoted' solely and alone to the prosperity and peaceful development of our Fatherland.
Sir, it was the Kaiser who uttered those words, and he says further on:

More than ever, unibedief and discontent raised their head. It may happen, though God forbid, that you may have to fire on your own parents and1 brothers. Prove your fidelity, then, by your sacrifice.
Would you not think that had been written for the present situation in the Dominion of Canada? Sir, knowing, as you have reminded me, that I should say nothing against the legislation which has been , passed by this Parliament, let me say at least that I regret its enactment. To my mind it is not only a violation of the rights of the people, but it is un-4 p.-m. patriotic, anti-Canadian, and anti-British.
We have been told, Sir, on several occasions, that we do not show enough loyalty. We have been told that we were not fulfilling our duty as we should in the present conflict. We have been told also, that there were many in this country who have given the best examples of loyalty. I remember a few years ago sitting in the press gallery, a post of honour from which, according to circumstances, I rwas forced to step down to where I am to-day, that a discussion took place in this House, and we heard of several men specially mentioned for their loyalty. I will only mention by name a few of those men, because I want to be brief. I remember that the then Minister of Militia gave us as ian example of loyalty and of devotion to the British Empire the name of a man who had refused any salary to work for the Empire's interests. That man was doing the Empire's work, it is said, from mere patriotism, and his name was Mr. Allison. I remember, also, that at that time they were boosting the name of a man, Sir Joseph Flavelle, who was also refusing any salary, or refusing to accept any money from the British Empire. No, Sir, that man would not accept any money from the British Empire; he was giving his services'on the ground of loyalty and nothing else. Think of Joseph Flavelle giving his services without any indemnity! The man whom we know now would apply the methods of Shylock to his mother's breast if by doing so he could1 pile up a little more money. There were other men-and I hope, Sir, that I am not speaking disrespectfully when I am not speaking of an Act of Parliament passed1 by members of this House -who boasted of their loyalty >and devotion to the British Empire, and they were tue two greatest scoundrels this country has ever produced-Mackenzie and1 Mann. It is rather surprising to learn that these

very men are still before Parliament asking for more of the people's money. There are others I could name, but these are sufficient for to-day. These men have been held up to us as examples of loyalty and devotion to the British Empire. Well, if to be loyal to the British Empire it is necessary to follow in the steps of these men, I will never be loyal to the British Empire. And I will say further, that if all those who have made the British Empire great and glorious, as it is, if all1 those who have immortalized England',-Nelson, Wellington. Wolfe, Roberts, Kitchener, and those who are making history to-day-were told that such men as those I have mentioned have been branded as examples of loyalty and as descendants of their blood, they would simply tell you, Mr. Speaker, that they were- not descendants of their blood, they were not even the foam or the slime of it.
I listened the other day to the Budget speech of the Acting Minister of Finance, and, as was stated yesterday by the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux), I think the acting minister was more of a mouthpiece than anything else on that occasion, I think that that speech was framed up in the land with which we were to have no truck or trade, and does not represent the personal opinions1 of the hon. gentleman. I cannot understand-I may be wrong-how the amount of our national debt could be specified with exactness by the acting minister. I remember that, two years ago, the Hon. Mr. Pugsley forced an answer from the Minister of Finance. We were -told what our liabilities to England were in the present war, that we would have to contribute in proportion to the number of men we sent to the front, compared with the number of men sent by England. We were also told that not a shell would explode on the front without Canada paying her contribution. I do not know whether I am misinterpreting what I heard !at that time, but if I am right, it seems to me impossible for the Acting Minister of Finance to state exactly what our debt situation is to-day. We are told that we will have to pay proportionately to the number of soldiers we have at the front compared with the number that England has. If England has five millions, and we have five hundred thousand, would it be wrong to think that we would be Liable for one-tenth of the war expenditure? We are bound certainly to pay a certain part of it. How can we know exactly to what proportion we are bound? Is there any understanding

*which has heen communicated to the House as to exactly where we stand on that question? I do not think so. I think that we are living in a desert absolutely on that question, and that neither the Acting Minister of Finance nor any one else can state where we stand. I say that not to find fault in any way with the Acting Minister of Finance, but 'because it is the right of the people of this country to know exactly where we stand. The Government is asking the people every year for hundreds of millions of dollars. They tell us the money will be loaned to England, that it will yield a good rate of interest; and that some day it will come back to us. The Prime Minister stated the other day that he thought there was a little balance in our favour; but there is nothing certain about that. Do you not think, Mr. Speaker, it only fair that the public should be informed of the exact situation?

For the past year or more the arrangement with the Imperial Government is that we pay the British Government the equivalent of, I think, $1.25 per day per man for the upkeep of our troops, and that arrangement has not been interfered with, so it is an exact amount. That includes also the equipment required for our men and our proportion of the munitions.
That amount covers the whole thing?
Yes.
I did not understand it that way when the Prime Minister referred to it.
I am not speaking definitely of the exact amount per day. It is either $1.20 or $1.25, but which I do not pretend to say exactly.

The only point in my mind was whether the amount .covered' all expenditures for munitions .and eo' on. I understand by the answer of the acting minister that we will not be called upon to pay any more than $1.25 or something like that.
Coming to another point, the Government claim that our credit stands good. May I tell hon. gentlemen opposite that I ao not agree absolutely with that statement. Not a month ago, the Prime Minister and the acting Minister of Finance went to Washington. For what purpose? We do not know exactly; we can only suppose. How is it that immediately after their return the cost of exchange between the two countries, which was at seveneighths of one per cent when they left for Washington, jumped to two per cent? Does this not indicate that they had to show their cards before the officials of the American Exchequer? The member for Kamouraska (Mr. E. Lapointe) suggests that it would be better for the country il those hon. gentlemen had stayed here.
It is represented that the cost of floating the Victory Loan, which amounted to over $400,000,000, was about one and one-quarter per cent, or $5,000,000. Papers supporting the Government expressed the view that that was a fair and honest cost, and that the people ought to be satisfied. With that I do not agree. It must not be forgotten that this cost of $5,000,000 was incurred in floating a loan not for $400,000,000, but for $150,000,000, and that if the people had subscribed only $150,000,000, as they were asked' to do, the cost would have been the same. The cost, therefore, of floating a loan of $150,000,000 amounted to $5,000,000, or three and one-third per cent, and when the Government float their next loan for $500,000,000 in a few months, the cost, if they proceed as, they did with the last loan, will be $16,666,000, at three and one-third per cent, rather than $6,250,000 at one and one-quarter per cent.
Just a word with regard to the coal question, in which the people of the province of Quebec are specially interested. In past years the freight rates on coal coming into Quebec from Nova Scotia and New Brunswick was $1.80 per ton. In 1916 the rate was increased by the then Minister of Rail- [DOT] ways to $3.20 per ton, making it prohibitive for the people of the province of Quebec, to import coal from New Brunswick or Nova Scotia. This condition is unjust to the province of Quebec, and should be remedied at once. The Acting Minister of Finance knows as well as I do that an extraordinary situation exists with regard to soft coal. The Intercolonial is using and will probably require large quantities of soft coal. This coal has been brought in from the United States where it was formerly purchased at the rate of $10.25 per ton f.o.b. Montreal. This year a quantity of that coal was bought at $7.85 f.o.b. Montreal, and hauled from Montreal to Campbellton, a distance of 464 miles. The cost of that haulage should not be more than $3.40 per ton, making the cost of the coal $11, whereas if the coal had been bought in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick the cost at the mine would not exceed $4 per ton, and the cost of hauling, as fixed by the former Minister of Railways, $3.40,

representing .a total of $7.40 per ton, and a saving to the country of at least $3 per ten. Why has this matter not been taken into consideration? The province of Quebec is entitled to protection in this respect as well as any other province. If proper steps were taken to safeguard our interests with regard to this coal, hundreds of thousands of dollars, which the Acting Minister of Finance so .badly needs, would be saved. We have hired the services of a fuel controller and of an American expert whom we have been paying $24,000 a year-
Well, it is fair to say that wa have been hiring the services of an expert on coal.
I did not deny that.

speakeroldname: Mr. R. H. BUTTIS (South Cape Breton and Richmond) :
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, referring to the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. Gladu) when he was called to order for his statement in connection with the War-time Elections Act, although I think his assertion was intended as a retort, I really regard it as a very high compliment to yourself. I have no doubt it was intended to refer to the soldiers' vote, and if the soldiers' vote was instrumental in electing you, I think the hon. member's, assertion was a very high compliment, for I assure you, iSir, I would sooner take my seat with a very small majority contributed by the soldiers' vote than come here by acclamation from a constituency of slackers. I do not intend to make any reference whatever to many of the somewhat excited remarks that have passed from one side of the -House to the other in regard to both racial and religious matters. I have long ago come to the conclusion that such a course is anything hut wise. Such remarks may be carried on as long as may be, hut in the end, racial and religious matters are albout the only victims. It is, therefore, somewhat out of keeping in this House that such remarks should be hurled across the floor and it would -be well if they were discontinued for all time.
The hon. member for North Cape Breton and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie), in his speech the other evening, referred to some secret- I think, mythical-agreement between hon. members, both Liberal and Conservative, on this side of the House, as to the tariff. I have only to say that, ii such an arrangement was ever made, I never heard of it previously to the opening of this House or to debate upon the Budget, and it is hard for me to understand why such an agreement should be made. As far as 1 can see, we -are all tariff men, we are all protectionists when in office. Even on the other side of the House, hon. members are protectionists when they are in power. It is only when they are in Opposition that they talk free trade. I remember some years ago when, previously to 1896, the last Conservative Government was in power, I was

then in the early days of my political inclinations, and I -was an ardent free trader,
I read the speeches of the then right hon. leader of the Opposition, the late Sir Richard 'Cartwright, and of many others, and from their speeches on free trade and their denunciation of high tariffs, I was led to believe that, on their accession to power, we would have a free trade Government, and that, under such a regime, great manufactures would grow up in this country; that the Northwest would be opened up with a rapidity unknown before; that small villages would become towns; that towns would become cities, and that cities would extend their borders. In fact, we were led to believe that, under the benign influences of this almost heaven-born policy, old men would be rejuvenated and old maids made marriageable. My hon. friends did not come into power altogether on their trade policy, but they did come in on a side issue; and if we are to take the words of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) they, during their regime, reduced the tariff by 71-100ths of one per cent. That was the degree of free trade to which they were prepared to go. When they were defeated in 1911, they immediately again became free traders. This reminds me very much of the old couplet:
When t'he devil was siok, the devil a monk would be;
When the devil got well, the devil a monk was he.
From my constituency over 4,000 young men volunteered for the front* and before 'conscription was spoken of they were in Flanders. Many of them are now home maimed. Many of them have made the supreme sacrifice in Flanders. I have heard from those who have returned many an interesting story about the condition of affairs at the front, about all the hardships they have had to- endure. The other night, while some free trade speeches were being made, I was thinking of certain stories that I had heard, and I was picturing to myself some of the scenes that had been depicted to me by those returned soldiers. I could see before me the condition of affairs as it had been described, and I was picturing those young men there in the trenches with the great cannons booming all around them, with shrapnel bursting in the air over them, and with machine gun and rifle bullets whistling on all sides. Perhaps at the gray of the morning the order was given for them to scale the parapet and take the front trenches of the enemy, and in No Man's Land he that fell and was instant-104
ly killed was perhaps not the unluckiest. Others lie bleeding the whole day long, suffering agonies compared with which the Cross itself, if I may say so without irreverence, was mercy. In the midst of my reverie, when I ivas thinking of the sacrifices made by parents such as those in the county of Cape Breton, where five mothers have sent twenty sons to the trenches, where two mothers who had sent four sons each, had each lost three, I was aroused by my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) deploring the five cent tax on the poor man's pipe and the ten cent tax on the old lady's cup of tea, and I thought then what different conceptions some people have of the sacrifices we are called upon to make in this war. Ten cents a pound on tea i3 surely an awful sacrifice for one old lady to make, when compared with the sacrifice of four sons by a mother. Did the terrible disparity, the awful misproportion, never occur to my hon. friend as he talked about the poor man's pipe and the old lady's cup of tea, and about these old ladies having been a factor in electing this Government?
He preached free trade, but it was not the kind of free trade hon. gentlemen opposite practised when they were in power. He said the Liberals had reduced the duties on steel during their regime. That is quite true, but if protection can be corrupt, they resorted to the most corrupt form of protection when they Temoved, or partially removed, the duty on steel, for they granted a bonus on a sliding scale to last for ten years. Let me give another example of how sincere hon. gentlemen opposite are in their professions about free trade and protection. The right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) said in 1897:
If we know the hearts and minds of our people at present, I think I am not making too wide a statement when 1 say that the general feeling in Canada is not in favour of reciprocity. There was a time when Canadians would have given many things to obtain the American market. There was a time when the market of the great cities of the Union was the only market we tad, but those days are passed and over now. We are not dependent on the American market now.
In 1907, in a speech at the Imperial Conference, he said:
There was a time when we were wanting reciprocity with the United! States, but our efforts and our offers were put aside and *negatived. We have said good-bye to that trade and' we now put ail our hopes on the British trade.
And justly so. I do not think the right hon. gentleman ever made a truer pro-

Mr. Speaker, I have no desire to prolong this debate, because I think all the questions involved have been already discussed at considerable length, but there are some matters in connection with this Budget which I have not yet heard any person mention,1 and which are of vital importance in connection with the affairs of the country. For that reason I trust that the House will bear with me while I refer briefly to those questions, and pass them on to the Government in the 'hope that they will receive consideration.
The Budget which we are discussing, as we all know, is the annual financial statement. I have heard quite a number of Budgets disbursed an Parliament, and the procedure is that when the Minister of Finance comes down to the House on that occasion he presents a statement of his stewardship during the past year. He states what the expenditures and revenues have been, and how much the revenue exceeded the expenditure, or, if there has been undue expenditure, what the balance is on the other side. The Finance Minister also takes occasion to estimate the amount of money that will be required for the various public services during the coming year, and then summarizes the various sources from which he hopes, by the imposition of taxation, to meet those expenditures. If additional expenditures are required, he indicates the direction from which he hopes to receive the necessary revenue to meet those expenditures.
Now, the Acting Finance Minister made a speech which, to my mind, was a model of clearness. Personally, I regret very much indeed that the Finance Minister himself was unable to be present. Knowing the tremendous amount of work and labour which has devolved upon that hon. gentleman since the beginning of the war, it was not to be expected that a man of his

physique could stand such a strain continuously. There is no doubt that so far in the financial history of the war, the Minister of Finance has met the situation. When confronted with almost unsurmountable obstacles he has overcome them, obtained the necessary funds, and in that respect has displayed great capacity. In the hon. gentleman who recently delivered the Budget speech, we have a worthy successor of Sir Thomas White. The Budget was excellent in its clearness of detail and lucidity of exposition, dealing with the expenditures of the past and the possible exexpenditures during the coming year. The Acting Finance Minister also very clearly outlined the new methods of taxation. But there was one omission from his speech, which he must have overlooked, although it has always appeared in previous Budgets, and that was the estimated amount of revenue expected to be derived .from the new taxes. 'Now, the present Administration is a Union Government, we are not supposed to -be attachedi particularly to one side of politics or the other, and, naturally, we would expect to be enlightened as to whether the Budget was a Union Government Budget or not. I regret to say that in my judgment the Budget which was submitted to the House a few days ago is not a Union Budget.	;
In the first place, if the Budget were a Union Government Budget the taxation would be collected, to some extent, equally from our two principal sources of revenue. At the present time some of our revenue is derived, from direct taxes, such as the income tax and the super tax and that constitutes what is known as a free trade or international method of taxation. We also receive a large amount of revenue from customs and excise duties,
5 p.m. which form wh.at is currently known a's the protection, the national or indirect system of taxation. Now, if the present Administration were in reality a Union Government the new taxation would, as I have already said, be collected to some extent equally from the two sources of revenue to which I have referred1; but that course has not been followed. I have looked very carefully over the statement of the Acting Minister of Finance, and I find that the new taxation applies' almost entirely to incomes. It is true that a tax has been imposed' on tea, coffee and tobacco, which will bring in some additional revenue. None of these articles, however, are produced to any extent in Canada, and the placing of any taxes what-;[Mr. Ctorrie.I
ever upon goods produced) in this country has been carefully avoided. To my mind that is not a proper system of raising additional revenue from the country. I may have my own views as to that, but I say that when you are applying added1 taxes to income only, you aie adopting the Free Trade method of taxation. Why should we have such a Free Trade Budget, and why, in the application of taxes, should we have recourse to only one onerous form of taxation? We are standing on the threshold of the fourth year of the war, which may be prolonged for another two years, we may have to raise additional money yet, and we have consistently, in the Budget, avoided a source of enormous revenue to this country, we have avoided the imposition of taxation that would .bear upon the people with scarcely any pressure at all, namely, .an addition to the customs tax.
In the first place, I would say this to the Acting (Minister of Finance: In looking over the blue books I find that the percentage of taxation upon imports this year is something like seventeen per cent, whilst in 1916 the percentage w.as over twenty per cent. In other words, the taxation on imports had been reduced three per cent during the war, whereas if it hadjoeen increased by 'that amount this year it would have yielded something like $25,000,000 to the country. Furthermore, had we adopted an increase of ten per cent it. would have yielded the enormous sum of $80,000,000 of additional revenue. For that reason I .say that we are eliminating and neglecting a most important source of revenue. I may be told that a taxation of twenty-seven per cent on imports is too much. I do not agree with that for the simple reason that the average in the United States is nearer fifty per cent. They are not neglecting any source of revenue over there, they are exploiting every source of revenue. Therefore, after examining the Budget, with all due regard to the Acting Finance Minister, and the manner in which his taxation proposals were framed, I must come to the conclusion that this is a Free Trade (Budget, .and deliberately framed as such, and that as far as the manufacturing and other industries of this country are concerned, we might as well roll up the industrial map on the wall. Why do I say that? I will give the House my reasons as briefly as I can, bearing in mind the fact that hon. gentlemen on both sides are anxious to get on with business. Why should we eliminate the source of revenue to which I have referred? Why

should we, instead, take away the profits of manufacturers and tax the people directly more and more every year? There is no particular merit in an income tax. The only claim to merit which an income tax finds among the people of England is that when they .are taxed on their income they will know how much they are paying and devote more attention to the administration of public affairs. During the war, when we have to raise such enormous sums, would it not be logical that we should place taxation where the people would feel the burden the least? To my mind the idea of playing free trade, as against protection, during the war, is exploded as far as this country is concerned.
The idea of free trade and protection is busted so far as this war is concerned. We have had to eliminate a great many of these old ideas. I am appealing to men of common sense in this House, and those who have studied economics know very well that it is only a matter of a few years since the gold standard as a basis for currency was accepted as an axiom, and no country was supposed to issue paper money unless it had a gold dollar in its treasury to meet a paper dollar. When the war broke out all those theories of the schoolmen, whose ideas of finance which had been propounded for years by the professors of Oxford, Cambridge and other universities, were swept away within the first two weeks, and Great Britain found herself compelled to go on a fiat money basis. England had to take tea paper, print her currency on this tea paper, and hand it out as money. Fortunately, they struck the secret of success so far as financing the country was concerned. I remember when the hon. member for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) used to come into this House and declare that we ought to issue paper *money. We all looked upon him as a heretic, a greenbacker, a man who wanted fiat money. To-day, every country in the war, with the exception of the United States, is on a paper basis, and it is only a matter of a few months until the. United States will be on a paper basis also. That is to say, the country promises to pay on paper, which paper takes the place of gold, and is not redeemable in gold during the war. We have had to revise our views, and a great change has come over the thinking community in England and every country. It is as if some new discovery had been made, such, for instance, as the discovery that the earth was round instead of flat. We all know that for centuries
professors preached the doctrine that the earth was flat, until suddenly one man advanced the view that it was round, and the discovery of the telescope proved that it was round. Nobody holds the opinion any longer that the earth is flat except a very few cranks. In the same way our preconceived notions of finance on the eve of the war are all going to be changed.
I think I have clearly established that we are on the threshhold of these great changes and we have to face that situation. We have in our imports, a source of taxation from which, if we took one-quarter as much in duties as do the United States, would give use at least eighty or ninety million dollars additional revenue every year.
There is nothing new in taxes; the world has used all methods of taxation. The first taxation ever adopted, I understand, was a hut tax which is still used in Africa amongst the primitive savages. They pay a hut tax to the colonial governments. The lottery system is another method. That system has been dropped out of consideration by the English-speaking people, although I understand it is used in some foreign countries. Another method of taxation is that on business transactions. It was put forward by some of the press, we were to have this here, that there should be a stamp on every business transaction. That is the alcavala of Spain, and its effect was to ruin business and to destroy industry and trade in Spain, and to make that country poverty stricken. We must not adopt that system. My idea is that we must adopt every reasonable expedient, because we need large sums of money, and the first thing we should consider is to find a system that will bear as lightly as possible on the shoulders of the people during the war. There are people going around the country endeavouring in every possible way to contrive something to make the people here feel there is a war on. Some people want to take away our tea, others our bacon, others want to take 90 per cent of our incomes; and in every possible way they are devising means to make the people feel that they are at war. If I were the German Emperor and wanted the people of this country to be directed in a certain channel which would make them tired of this war and cease to support it, I would adopt a policy, not only in taxation but in other things, that would stir up resentment. I think it is a great mistake that the minister omitted to add a substantial percentage to the customs duties of the country.

There are two methods of taxation known to the world, direct 'and indirect. One of the old fashioned direct taxes is a head tax or a poll tax. That would get a very large sum of money, 'hut *would be unpopular. There is also the taxation on real property. And the very reason that England has a tax on incomes is because the landowners would never stand for a tax on their property. We know that a few years ago Lloyd George proposed to impose a tax oh landed property, and they were all up in arms. It is not necessary for us to follow those methods; the methods for us to follow are those adopted by the United States. With reference to the income tax itself, it works out very unfairly. The man who pays an income tax on rentals, for instance, can pass that tax oai to the tenants, tout the man whose revenue is derived from his labours cannot pass the tax on, and therefore it bears heavily on him and his family. There is no particular merit in an income tax any more than in a hut tax; they are only methods of deriving revenue. For our country the income tax is the moat dangerous system we can adopt. England has raised large sums of money in this way, but England is beginning to realize that there is a limit. The 'United States after the war of the Revolution and the War of 1812, adopted the system of taxation on imports, because that was a method' which assisted the country in selling as much in a foreign market and buying little, keeping down the trade balance. By 1837 the cost of the Revolutionary War and of the War of 1812-14 were fully paid up. About the same time England was engaged in the Napoleonic Wars, and as near as I can find out, the cost of those wars is still toeing borne by the British people and they are paying interest on it still. Is that a policy for us to follow? When a tremendous amount of money is going to be charged to us, should we not adopt the policy of the United States, and struggle as (best we can to get rid of this burden inside of ten or fifteen years? It is a great mistake not to have adopted the policy of adding an additional amount of taxes on imports. Take the case of trade: In addition to the expenditure on the war, which is one of the dark clouds on the horizon, there is also the war itself. I have no idea in my mind at all as to when the war is going to end, and whilst many members of this House and many of my friends are pessimistic over war conditions at the present time, knowing every foot of that country as I do and knowing that all that territory which the Germans took back a few .days ago, 
I know that a great deal more of territory was held by them in 1914, I am still confident of the success of our arms.
They have not gained one foot of new territory. They are stopped and I am satisfied that it is only a question of time when they will be driven back. But we must face the necessity of constantly raising more men. I am glad the Government has adopted a policy for men which has some ginger in it. We must, however, get a little more ginger in our finances and not be afraid to put a tax on imports simply because one or two members on this side of the House happen to be theoretical free traders. I have listened to the avowed free traders on this side of the House with care and find they are reasonable men, men of great ability. I am sure that if any question is put fairly to them they will be satisfied to do what they consider to be Canada's duty. Why should we impose heavy direct taxation upon the people when we can get three times the money without their knowing anything about it or feeling the burden? The United States has constantly followed the protective financial policy laid down by Alexander Hamilton. By 1890 they had paid for the expenses of the Civil war, whereas Great Britain under free trade has not yet paid off the expenses of even the South African war, which are a burden every year to their people. The people of the United States are wise and practical; they do not run to fads; they take a common sense View of things; they do business without much regard to sentiment. Why do I say that we should add a tax on imports now? That may seem like heresy to a free trader, but there is no such thing as freedom of international trade at this time-. A great change has come over all states. There is no free interchange of products. Nations are placing an embargo on many things that formerly came into their country. What is the use of having free trade with the United States if that country will not trade with us at all? Almost everything is embargoed that might go from Canada to the United States; we cannot sell an axe handle there, let alone a bushed of wheat, unless the Government of the United States grant us a special license. The result of that policy during the past year is that we have bought unlimited quantities of goods from the United States-something like $600,000,000 or $700,000,000 worth-and we cannot sell one dollar's worth of goods to them to pay our debts^-nor can we borrow and fund our debt. In view of this fact, how

can any sane man say that -we should stick to old ideas and old doctrines? There is a proposal on the Order Paper to give to Minister of Trade and Commerce the right to place an embargo on the importation of non-essential products into Canada from the United States. That is one way of avoiding the difficulty that confronts us,_ but another way would be to impose a heavy customs tax on all things that come from the United States. But we are in debt to the United States some five hundred million. They have refused to lend us the money to pay off our trade balance, but suppose they lent us the money, what right has any loyal Canadian woman to buy an American pair of shoes at $10 and make it necessary for the Minister of Finance to go to Washington and borrow $10 for thirty years at interest in order to pay for them? If a farmer's wife in the West buys from the United States a Chicago cook stove at $50 the Minister of Finance, if he can borrow in Washington -which he cannot just now-will have to borrow $50 in the United States to pay for that stove, and every man, woman and child in this country will have to pay 6 per cent interest on that $50 for thirty years. To do these things is absurd when we can buy these articles in this country with Canadian paper money instead of paying gold for thbm in the United States. If this condition continues and our trade balance keeps going up, we will owe the United States $1,000,000,000 on our trade balance before the war is over. When the Allies meet in final conference to adjust their balances the United States is going to exact that $1,000,000 in some form or other. We haven't the gold; how can we pay? They will not lend us the money; will we have to give territory for it? United States is a great country, and we all welcome her into the war. But, speaking on my responsibility as a member of this House, I submit that United States has failed to recognize Canada as being on the same plane as the other Allies, so far as war finances are concerned. Everybody knows that. We are not treated even as neutrals.

Is that the fault of the United States? Did not the United States offer to deal with us on the same basis that they were dealing with England? Did they not offer us orders for munitions if we wanted to accept them?

I know the United States gave Great Britain an order for munitions a
few months ago through Secretary Baker to the extent of $1,300,000,000, in order to enable Great Britain to make munitions and get out of the debt she owed the United States.
And we could have had the same.

If that same policy could be adopted here we should very soon be free of our debt to the United States. However, the matter is beyond me. Some of these boards and commissions, over which we seem to have no control but which seem to be spending plenty of money for us all the time, are simply stop-logs, in the current of our trade. No man who is a profiteer or who has. been in the shell game should ibe put on a board or commission that has to do with our foreign trade. I do not like to name anybody. We all know who are on some of these boards. We know that they have factories in Canada manufacturing things for which they are liable to get orders from, the United States, and that they have moved machinery from Canada to the United States in order to make munitions. They want to be in strategic positions.
Did they not go to the United States because they were not allowed to bring goods from the United States into Canada?

Well, I do not know -as
to their going to the United States because they could not get orders for munitions here. I was told by a Montreal man who has an order for shells; from the United States that to get that order he had to pay 7J pear cent commission to the Imperial Munitions Board. I do not think that any foreign institution in this country has the right to impose taxation upon the people of Canada. That should be done by Parliament alone. As far as the munitions business is concerned, the money raised by the Victory Loan in Canada during the last year was divided between munitions and wheat. Great Britain was unable to finance us. They said: If you want to make munitions, you must do your own financing. We must have wheat; we cannot give you the money to pay for it; you will have to raise the money yourself for the wheat-and we did so.
i I 'think it is most hateful for members of Parliament to be provincial. I am a son of the great province of Ontario. We grow big men there; we try to let the people enjoy their full rights; we wish that justice Ibe done to every one.

We are struggling hard to get out of the clutch of the so-ca/lled interests. We are an example to the whole world in public ownership institutions and in public-owned industries that are great and successful. Seventy-five per cent of the Victory Loan was raised in the province of Ontario. Seventy-five per cent of the munition orders went east of the Ottawa river. Seventy-five per cent of the grain and foodstuffs orders went west of Fort William. Yet Ontario has been constantly attacked by hon. members. You would think we were a lot of selfish people. You have never heard us complain about these orders in the press of Ontario, and every man in business in Ontario knows very well that we got the small end. We have tried to do our duty. We know that it is impossible for this country ever to achieve the greatness and the status that it should achieve if we are going to preach constantly sectionalism, class hatred, and stir up trouble between the provinces. We cannot have that. We must forget all those things, and now, of all times, is the period when we should forget them.
We are constantly charged, because, unfortunately, two or three so-called trusts have their headquarters in Ontario, that we are robbing the western farmers. I shall refer to some of these trusts, and it is just as well for us to have the matter spoken of openly in the House. Let us take the question of agricultural implements. There are in Ontario, and also in the Western Provinces, many concerns manufacturing agricultural implements. But there are agricultural implements and agricultural implements. The one item that stands out most of all is that which is controlled by a large trust. I refer to the binder used by the farmer. The question of reaping machines and binders is constantly being raised by the farmers. They say: Everybody is taking advantage of us, because we are taxed by protectionists on our binders. This is a matter of regret to every manufacturer, great and small, in Ontario, aye, and in Quebec, where they must have in the future greater manufactories, if they are going to retain their population, because they have not the agricultural land to support their population without the help of industries; they must depend on industries. Every legitimate manufacturer in Ontario regrets that there is such a thing as a binder industry in Ontario. It is of no use whatever to any other industry in Ontario than itself.
All the goods that go into the manufacture of a binder, for instance, the wood that
[IMr. Currie.]
goes into the tongue of it, or into the platform of it, the canvas, the tacks, the pig iron, are brought into this country free of duty, and those small manufacturing concerns in Canada who are manufacturing and who could manufacture those parts legitimately, do not get a cent out of the business. It is doubly protected. No other industry in Canada is protected in that way. Take the question of ploughs. Last year over $2,500,000 worth of ploughs were brought into this country. There is in the world no better plough made than the plough that is made in Canada, A plough is a very low priced article. There are in my province dozens of concerns manufacturing ploughs, but the race hatred cry has so grown in the West and the farmers are so stirred up against our ploughs and other small articles that we are legitimately trying to manufacture in order to support the population in our towns and villages, that they are boycotting our Ontario manufacturers, and they will not purchase our ploughs. What merit is it for a farmer in the West to buy an American plough at $25 or $30, and then send the Minister of Finance down to Washington to borrow money on that amount at 6 per cent for thirty years, simply because the farmer wants to buy an American plough? I have here a long list of articles. Last year we imported over $1,000,000 worth of cot.ton socks which could have been made ' in Montreal, where large quantities of socks are manufactured. Last year fully $400,000,000 worth of manufactured goods were brought into Canada which could have been manufactured by Canadian concerns.
The manufacturers of Canada have, during the last four years, been constantly subjected to unfair competition by the Americans. Let me point out an article that is free of duty, and that is made in this country, so that we need not become involved in any question of tariff in regard to it. I refer to barbed wire. The western farmers buy an average of 125 tons of barbed wire a day. The manufacture of that in Canada would give employment to about 5,000 people. Those people would be eating western wheat, whereas the people in the United States cannot eat western wheat, because the United States will not allow any western wheat to enter that country. There is an embargo on it. But, as I say, we import that barbed wire. Barbed wire has two prices in the United States. There is an " ordered " price of $3.80; there also is a " spot delivery " price, which is an

export price to the Allies and all other countries in the world of $4.75. If you live in the United States and you want a car of barbed wire, you go to the United States Steel Corporation and you ask them the price. They will say: "Well, we shall give it to you at $3.70 on order, or if you want 'spot' stuff, we cannot give it to you at that price." You say: "If I order it, when can I have it?" They will tell you: "You can have it after the war." But your wire was broken down and the cattle are running around your ranges, and you want the barbed wire right away, so you ask them: "Have you any "spot" wire? They say: "No, but John Jones across the street has some of our wire, and you can get some of it if you want an immediate order." If you go there, you will find that you will have to pay $4.70 to $4.80 for it. I know these are facts that I speak of. The documents are in Canada to prove them. If, however, a western Canadian jobber went down to Pittsburg and asked the United States Steel Corporation what barbed wire was worth, they would say: "The 'order' price is $3.40." He would ask them: "Can I get some?" They would say: "Where do you live?" He would reply: "I live in Saskatchewan." Then they would say: "All right, you can- have it right away at $3.40." They thus flood this country not only with barbed wire, but they dump every other manufactured article which can be shoved into Canada on what is called an "order" price. That has been the unfair policy of the manufacturers of the United States. Some of the large trusts in the United States have tried this two price system on various other commodities. They have applied it on coke, of which they virtually have a monopoly. If you wanted to buy "order'' coke, you could get it at $3 a ton, and have it delivered after the war. But if you wanted coke for immediate delivery you had to pay $12 a ton for it. The Government here was negligent in not taking cognizance of the two prices system in the United States, and stopping its application here, but they were more negligent than that, because if a good stiff customs duty were put on those articles it would have brought in to our treasury from seventy to eighty million dollars a year which would have enabled us to pay a hundred million dollars of the four hundred million dollars that we spent annually on the war. In 1916-17, we paid $100,000,000; in 1917-18, we shall pay not more than $50,000,000. If we were able to carry on our taxation in
such a way as to pay on this war a hundred million dollars every year, inside of ten years after the termination of the war Canada would be free from all war debt. 1 am sure that every man who gives a thought to the finances of this country would say that is the proper method of carrying on taxation.
I wish to refer now' to other things that are giving us a great deal of trouble. I refer to the proposal to grant the Minister of Trade and Commerce the right to embargo imports. We must do either one of two things, We must make up our minds to go behind the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) as one man and say: We give you full authority, for every year from now until the war is over, to put an embargo upon goods coming into this country from countries that will not trade with us, or else we must insist that the Government take the other method of imposing a stift tax on goods coming from countries of that description. Otherwise Canada will be on the auction block after the war is over; we shall owe the United States so much money that we shall have to hand over to them British Columbia or Quebec or some other part of the country in payment. The manufacturers of Ontario, when they can meet the American manufacturers in a free market, are not afraid of their competition. In the manufacture of chains, for instance, Canadian manufacturers have discovered a method of making the chains automatically by electrically welding them.
What kind of chains?

Logging chains, cow chains, and other chains of that description, of which a very large quantity is used in the United States and Canada. These Canadian manufacturers went to the United States, and inside of five years, by this new method, put the American chain factories out of the running. That shows what the Canadian manufacturers can do when given a fair chance. Our manufacturers are not behind our soldiers in enterprise, energy or courage, and you know how good our soldiers are. All we want is a fair and square deal. We do not want to be constantly subjected to one-sided unfair competition.
Is the hon. gentleman of the opinion that a protective tariff operating to the advantage of eastern manufacturers operates equally to the advantage of western farmers? s

Certainly it does, because every extra mile the western farmer has

to send his -wheat-I am speaking now of after-the-war conditions,-represents a toll on him. If the farmer sold his wheat to the industrial workers nearby, we would save this extra freight, and be that much more in pocket. But there is such a thing as selling the hide for six pence and buying the tail back for a pound." The whole policy of the United States has been to build up home industries. Patriotic people in Canada are trying to do likewise. I am connected with a firm that has been manufacturing a line of goods that is shipped to .the four corners of the earth. They had a large shipment to make to Ceylon and India, and needed jute sacks in which to ship the goods. Hon. gentlemen will hardly believe me when I say that the city of Winnipeg, in competition with every other city in Canada that was asked to bid, took the prize and got the order for the jute sacks; and the jute sacks were made in Winnipeg, shipped to Ontario, -and then sent out to Ceylon and India. That is the condition that is going to obtain all over this country. Factories in the West are going to succeed as they are in the East. The province of Ontario has established a great trade with the province of Nova Scotia. There is more business done ibetween those two provinces, I believe, than between any other two provinces in the country, and it is because the province of-Nova Scotia with governmental assistance -has built up great iron and steel works-, -and were it not for these works the manufacturers of Ontario would not have been able during the last two years to carry on business for one-half of their time. We had to have pig iron and steel, and we received greater advantages from these works in Nova Scotia. So he would be a very unnatural son of Ontario or of Nova Scotia who would try to set up any barriers or clan hatred between these two provinces.
We must look thing-s in the face. The munitions business -at the present time is dying away, and our factories will have to go at other work very soon. I am sorry to say that in many r-espects the Imperial Munitions Board did not observe Pitt's great maxim that they must make war pay. The ex-Minister of Militia and Defence knew that maxim, and did his best to carry it out. Men in this -country who had made decent sums in the manufacture of munitions were thinking -of enlarging their factories, but during the last two years the prices imposed by the Munitions Board -have been so ridiculously low that
[Mr. Ourrie.1
these men have taken the orders at a great loss, and many of them have gone out of -business and are now ruined. Many of our manufacturers, through lack of munitions orders, are taking their plants out of the country -and working them in the United States. If the United States can give an order for one billion three hundred millions dollars worth of munitions to Great Britain, there is no reason why we should not get an order of reasonable size. What is the use of piffling with a forty or fifty million dollar order? That does not cut any figure. Last year we purchased close on to seven hundred million dollars' worth from the United States, and how -can we pay for those g-ood-s unless we get orders for a similar amount for munitions or goods of one kind or another from the United States? Otherwise we shall have to close up our factories and our working men will go to the States. I am not a munitions manufacturer, so I am not personally interested in the game, but I -am intensely interested in the success of my country. We have gone into this war, being a good loyal people, and we are now asking everybody to send their sons to the front under conscription. What do we -get o-ut of the war? What does Australia get out of it? She is going to get an Empire in the Pacific; the German empire in the Pacific will go to Australia.
What does .South Africa get? .She -also gets an empire, two empires, in fact in Africa. What does Egypt get? She is doing very little, she gave five million pounds to the war. What is five million pounds in comparison with the amount we are spending on the war? Egypt will get Palestine and Arabia. Italy will get Asia Minor. Every country of the Allies, is going to be in-damnified except Canada. The indemnity which the United States is looking for is world trade, for they cannot receive any territorial indemnity; neither can we. The only indemnity we can get is a business indemnity. Then, as solid business men, why should we not forget our petty squabbles about what some school man wrote in a book years ago? I heard the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) speaking on free trade last night, and he reminded me of the doctors a thousand years ago disputing on the -merits of, Aristotelian medicine as against experimental science.
I thought we were fighting for ideals and not for business.

We are fighting for an
ideal, and that ideal is freedom, parliamentary freedom. When Strafford- stood at the

Bar of the English House of 'Commons, charged -with trying to suppress parliamentary liberties in England, he urged in his defence, "I have given a Parliament to Ireland." What answer did Pym give him? He said, " Parliaments without parliamentary liberties are but a fair and pleasant way to greater servitude." Stick that under your hats, gentlemen. That is a good motto for us in this House. We are fighting for freedom, but we must not forget to have a little eye on what we are going to do at home after the war. We all know that after the American war there was heard all over the country the tramp of the boys in the blue overcoats on all the roads of the United States; they were soldiers out of a job. The outhouses, the fence corners were filled with soldiers begging their bread. The United States immediately grasped the situation and did everything they possibly could by a high tariff to get factories established to give employment to these men. 'That is why I am calling at tention to these matters now.
There will be three or four hundred thousand men coming home after the war, seventy-five per cent of whom are not farmers. Why, at one time at the front, there was a whole battalion of students, most of them in their third or fourth year- the Princess Pats, the brainiest men that ever stood in France.
The Princess Pat men were the highest type of men that ever set foot in France. Our battalions are composed of men of high educational attainments, men who can take their places in the factories, the mines or industrial institutions of the world. Why should we not help these men to secure profitable employment in industrial callings' at home, as well as to put them on farms? The majority of these men from Ontario, Quebec and Nova Scotia are skilled in industrial trades and employments, and if you insist on putting them on farms you are going to impose a very great hardship upon them. Is it not better that we should keep this country on an even keel? We should not build up one industry at the expense of others. In order that these men .and their families may have, their bread and butter assured to them in the time to come after they leave the army and are disbanded, we should try and make the war pay for itself new, build up factories all over the country so that these men when they come back will have employment and take the places of the women factory workers, because the women in many casesi, while filling the men's places for the present, will not continue to work in factories.
It is no use to talk about free trade, because there, is no such thing as free trade.
No man will stand up before me in this House and say that free trade is a possibility now in Canada foT a moment. The hon. member for Brome (Mr. MoMaster) knows very well the facts that stare him in the face. We are face to face with new conditions. With all our patriotism, with all our love of country, with all our love for those men who are now serving at the front, we are surely not going to divest ourselves- of .all our interest the moment these men come hack. Both our interest and our affection should teach us that it is our duty at the present moment to forget all this piffling about protection and free trade. We want to 'build up a country that will sell its- products to the world and buy as little as possible for the time, being. We can thus only get out of debt. Let political economy wait until we are past this great crisis. If we do that we will be in a better national position. If a 10 per cent customs tax were imposed on imports we would get at the very least $80,000,000. Nobody would be any the worse for that except those foolish women who buy American boots and those young fellows we see on the streets who are working in munition factories and who like to wear .some American collar or tie. Why should we support them in trading abroad?

I have 'been in this Parliament I have heard nothing but sneers, and expressions of scorn directed .at the manufacturers.
