The hon. the exMinister of Militia and Defence (Sir Sam Hughes) knows that that is true. Lloyd George, after another year, said: "Gentlemen, have you your plants free?" " Yes." I will continue the price of munitions on condition that you give me a quarter or a third "-I	forget iwhich-" of your
profits." Why should they not give him a third of their profits? He had given them a free plant and they were quite willing to give him a fair share of the profits. That is what took place in England. Now, what happened in Canada? When the Imperial Munitions Board was established they said to the manufacturer:	We want you to
make shells." The manufacturer said: "I have not any plant." " You will have to vet a plant."
We preceded England in that.	"

That is right, but it was dropped here when England took over the manufacture through the Imperial Munitions Board. The arrangement which was made by the late Minister of Militia and Defence 'to start the manufacturers of Canada making munitions, in justice to him, was borrowed by Mr. Lloyd George. There is no doubt about that, and we want to give the hon. gentleman full credit for that. The manufacturers of Canada and England do. But the Imperial Munitions Board said to the manufacturer: " Do you want to mal^ shells?" The manufacturer said: "Yes." " You must get your own plant and put it in. Alright. The directors of companies went to the banks and the bank directors stretched their imaginations a great deal and lent them the necessary money. But the directors of the companies had to go on the notes personally in almost every case in order that these plants might be put in. The prices for shells were very low, but still there was a margin of profit in it. No sooner had these manufacturers succeeded in showing a slight margin of profit for the first year than everybody in this country started yelling: " You are making too much profit out of this thing; the Government must take your profit." The Government have done so in the form of the supertax which has been imposed. I do not believe there is one out of a hundred corporation directors in this country who sleeps soundly at night. Why? They are a badly abused lot. 
If they go to the bank to borrow $100,000, they have to get down on their knees before they can get it, although in some cases the banks are very good. Some of the older banks are exceedingly good, but the company directors have to go on the notes of the company. What do they get out of that? If they get a ten dollar fee from their company for a meeting of directors, it is known all over the country. They have to go on the notes of these corporations, and if one fails to make any profit the directors have to make good the loss out of their own pockets. Do the shareholders have to pay that? No, they have paid up stock in their pockets, and like everybody else they have a kick at the directors. This country owes a great debt of gratitude to every director of a public company. If there are any people in Canada who have helped Canada to carry on the war, they are those men who are the directors of public companies and those carrying on manufacturing industries. Yet these men are constantly abused and are looked upon as outcasts, and as being unfit for ordinary society. I am ashamed to see this country forming small factions about this, that and the other thing.
I was the other day reading May, the well known authority on constitutional law, and he says the only safety for a country is partyism, that if you have not partyism you are going to have faction, and government will not be staple but will fall to pieces. Are you going to have in this country factions, differences and class hatreds, the farmer against the manufacturer, the manufacturer against the man who is working for him, and the labourer and the labour union against the manufacturer? Why should we begrudge a fair profit to the man who is at the head of a factory? There is no reason why we should. There is no reason why the directors of corporations and the captains of industry in this country should not be allowed to carry on their business as free, honest men, or why they should be constantly classed as rascals and renegades. It was faction and class hatred that ruined Russia. Where do you get your Victory Loan from?
You do not get it from those people who are going about the country crying down the manufacturers. The working class are sound and I must say for them, they have subscribed to the Victory Loan to the limit of their ability, just the same as any other class. The manufacturer also has subscribed, but in order to enlarge his factory, as is necessary in order to make pro-

vision for the future, he cannot willingly take all the .loans you offer him. What is the policy which has been adopted in England? There Lloyd Genrge has done what he could to help the manufacturers, his idea being that war should pay and that their co-operation was necessary towards the winning of the war. It is from these manufacturers he is getting money for his loans. The same policy is pursued in Germany where the government have aided the manufacturers to develop their industries, believing that in so doing they were helping to win the war. The Germans do not buy abroad, and buying at home use paper money. As long as they do this they can go on indefinitely. In this country, however, no man can make a dollar but what everybody joins in an attack upon him. I think it is time that sort of conduct was .stopped.
There is another phase of the Budget I wish to discuss, and that is the railway situation. Let me say that it is one of the most dangerous issues this country has to meet at the present moment. The war of. the railroads in Canada is far greater than ihe war of Great Britain on Germany at the present moment. It is well known to members who .sa't with me on this side of the House in the last Parliament, that we urged the policy on the Government of following the example of the Government of. Great Britain and relieving the railroads from the possibility of giving us any trouble during the war. What happened in Great Britain when the war broke out? There one-third of the railways were excursion lines and could not earn a dollar. Many of the large roads could carry on, but very few of the small ones could. The British Government very wisely called the heads of all these railways together and .said to them: "Form a board. Every railway in Great Britain is going into this board, and the directors will manage all the systems as one concern. All the money that comes in will be pooled/ in one pool, and the Government will see that every shareholder gets a return equivalent to what he has been receiving on his investment for the past three years." That was a very successful idea. For three years the Government of Great Britain successfully carried on the railways in that way, Although I cannot say what the results of last year's operations were, they have increased the earnings of the employees from time to time by what they call war bonuses. That is, instead of an increase in wages the Government would give them
a war bonus of ten per cent. In that way, as the cost of food went up the railwaymen's earnings kept pace with it, and the Government have done that after attending to all the wants of the debenture holders and the shareholders. Not only so, but the Government have carried free on those railways all their munitions and all the men that they needed at the front. We know that in 1914 all the British and all the Canadian soldiers got a free ticket on the railways to go and visit the localties where they came from, and it didn't cost the Government a farthing. We suggested the same thing should be done here, but the interests had too much control. For some reason, although many of us, including some able men, tried to do our best to get that policy carried out, we failed. The Government, however, succeeded in running us into a debt of thirty or forty millions a year that we have to pay, for these railways. No wonder the United States does not want to finance this country at the present moment, bearing in mind the improvident and wasteful policy we have pursued with railways. What has the United States Government done? The very moment they were involved in war they followed exactly the same course as Great Britain; they established a War Board to control their .railways exactly as Great Britain has done, and they are putting men of business ability at the head of their great departments. I have no hesitation in saying that if we had placed ourselves at the beginning of the war in the same condition as Great Britain did and given the management of our railways to that great Canadian, Lord Shaughnessy, he would have established operating traditions on all our roads. The first tradition that would have been emphasised on the employees would1 have been honesty, from the water-boy right up to the president. The second tradition that Lord Shaughnessy would have developed in the course of three weeks after he had taken charge, would have been loyalty to the road. Travel on the Canadian Pacific railway and say anything to a brakesman or a water-boy derogatory .to that road and the first thing you get is a sharp rebuff. That is loyalty. Every man feels that he is a part of that great machine, that he is doing a great public duty, and a great public service. He is not looking round to see if he can slink off and steal an hour from his employers, or get away into a corner and hide himself, but is doing his utmost to earn his pay. If we could have such a fine spirit established on every Canadian railroad there

bee; wherever they could find a subsidy they were prepared to build a road and bond it-and now we have to pay the piper.
They went to British Columbia also on [DOT]the principle that they must get an outlet on that coast. It was argued that elevators were to be built and that all the grain of the western provinces was to be sent from the Pacific coast around the Horn and the Cape of Hood Hope to feed the Englishmen. Of course .they never dreamed that when the grain crossed the equator the midge fly and the maggot would get into it; that every bushel of wheat which goes over the equator must be specially treated and disinfected in order that it may be transported without injury. That was all forgotten; there was millions on the Pacific coast, they thought, for any enterprising promoter who went there. So the road went from Edmonton through the Yellowhead Pass, never more than one hundred or two hundred yards from the National Transcontinental that we are [DOT]sweating blood to pay for. The line went as far west as the other side of Prince George. They thought they could get a lot of fine scenery that way; they turned down and took some of the scenery from the Canadian Pacific. As a matter of fact, I suppose the Canadian Pacific would have been glad to give them the heavy grades along the Thompson and Fraser rivers. They paralleled the Canadian Pacific down the Fraser valley, the Canadian Pacific on one side of the creek and the Canadian Northern on the other, and they landed at Vancouver. If it were possible to operate any of these roads as a double-track line, a great deal of trouble would be saved, operating expenses would be reduced, a smaller working staff would be sufficient, and less equipment would be required. The grades could be readjusted on the up-and-down tracks.. >One staff of superintendents and operators and one private car to trot round the country in, instead of three or four, would be sufficient. We find our-[DOT]selves in a difficulty so far as these roads [DOT]are concerned; we have to provide money; and there will be great difficulty in synchronizing operation. I always like to find historical parallels for peculiar incidents in history, but I cannot find in any country in the world a case that at all parallels that of Mackenzie and Mann. A man by the name of Law blew certain bubbles in France, but he did not constantly bleed the people because they benefited by his operations in the establishment of banks. He left the Bank of England and the Bank of France. He blew the South Sea bubble 
in England; but these Mackenzie and Mann bubbles beat anything I ever saw or heard of in history. We are stuck for something like $25,000,000 a year for these gentlemen. When anything ever happens around the corridors of [DOT] any legislative body in this country they have a lot of lawyers versed in the art of talking to members, and if you are a newly-elected member a very smooth gentleman offers you a cigar, gets into conversation with you and after a while wants to know your views on granting Mackenzie and Mann $50,000,000 of a bonus, or something of that kind. They operate amongst public men, the legislatures of the provinces and the Parliament of Canada. There is hardly a mile from the Behring -sea to the trenches in France would fail to disclose wrecks strewn by these two men. Everything that they touch has blown up. At first their stocks went flying up like a kite, and when the public set in and woke up they had nothing but the stick left. Take the street railway in Winnipeg, the stock of which at one time was about 200, and is now down to about 50. When they owned the Toronto street railway the stock went up to 150 or 180; to-day it is down to 50. They are out. Wrecks all the way-saw mills, coal mines, trawlers, saw mill companies, whaling companies. I am informed that the coal lands on Vancouver island for all time will be obliged to earn an extra tax of something like $2.50 a ton because of the operations of Mackenzie & Mann. Now they are broken, they say, and they want more money. Nobody seems to know where they lost their money, what latitude or longitude, but they want more.
This country has- entered into an agreement with them now to pay $10,000,000 for the rights of a road which is really in real financial difficulties. We have to take care of it by issuing short-term notes, and when we do get it, we shall hardly know what to do with this white elephant. No doubt, Mackenzie & Mann will come down to Ottawa after we pay them and want it back. I am credibly informed that those gentlemen are still in control of the Canadian Northern railway. I would have thought, when this country has used Mackenzie & Mann so well and has agreed to arbitrate their equity in the stock, a question which we really did not need to arbitrate at all, because we could have taken over the road under a mortgage; when we are so willing to hand them over $10,000,000, if they can only show us a reasonable

excuse for doing so-and some of their excuses are rather flimsy-that they would have the good grace to step out of the directorate and management of the company pending the conclusion of that investigation. I am told that Mackenzie & Mann are still in control of the Canadian Northern and direct its resources and enterprises. Furthermore, I understand that a very strong effort is being made to see that the control of the Consolidated Railway Companies of Canada is put into the hands of Sir William Mackenzie as general manager. This will need an Order in Council but the people of this country will rise in rebellion if anything of that kind occurs. We are tired of those gentlemen and their exploits. I have nothing personally against either of them. As a clannish Highland Scotchman, I would like to see them succeed. They have not, however, shown the slightest evidence of ability to manage public affairs, except to plunder the people. If a man had a good steam sawmill at any place along theiT line, they were not satisfied until they put another one in and beat him out of what he had. If a 'man had a coal yard out of which he was making money, they would put in another coal yard and destroy his business. It was nothing but a record of wrecks, as I said, from the Behring sea to the trenches. It is very hard for me to make these statements, but I have to speak the truth. It is difficult for a public man to tell the truth as he should do in a public place like this, but I am stating facts. We have to handle their derelicts. We have to pump the water out of those floating hulks of theirs. We have t0' get them into some shape again, and if we are going to do that, let us put in charge of therm somebody who has business ability, and let us see that the road is properly managed and is not to continue a streak of rust as it is at present.
What is the condition of the National Transcontinental, which is another problem we have to face? For a number of years I handled the financial Bills of the Grand Trunk Railway in the House of Commons, and I shall say this, that under the management then of Mr. Hays, and those men who came here, especially Mr. Wainwrigbt, an effort was made to put the old Grand Trunk on a first-class financial footing. Those men made that effort. They saw their troubles; they started in to pay up all their debts with debenture stock, which did not carry a mortgage against the road at all. Those debentures were sold in England, and
as bonds matured the mortgages were taken off that road until, at one period, before they started financing for the new railway in the West, I think there was only something like $8,000,000 worth of bonds against the whole road. That was a very small amount, the road being at that time valued at between fifty .and sixty million dollars: That was a splendid example of financing, unequalled by .any other road on the American continent at that time; but they got into the flotation business, the transcontinental fever, and they agreed to finance the greater portion of those roads in the West which connect with the Grand Trunk Railway. The result is that the shareholders of the Grand Trunk are now so much involved that it is almost hopeless for those who hold the debentures ever to expect to receive a dividend. Did this country put the shareholders in that position? No. Their own directors, whom they appointed with their own votes, put them into that difficulty. That road, or a portion of it, must be taken over, and, as far as I am concerned, I think the only solution of the matter is to deal fairly with those shareholders and take over the whole road. The East will then, if it is properly managed, take care of the West; it will help the West. The tremendous arteries the Grand Trunk has running into every town and village of the East, coupled with the western connections and the similar web of the Canadian Northern in the West-those two gigantic webs joined together will, to my mind, pay and can be made to pay.
Last year, however, we found ourselves in the face of a peculiar difficulty. Those roads were constantly running into debt, and the Canadian Pacific was constantly making money. Instead of adopting the plan in existence in the United States of pooling the roads, we must adopt some expedient, and the expedient adopted was to raise the rates on those roads by 15 per cent. As a shipper, I do not see anything wrong in an additional freight rate of ten or fifteen per cent, because we must realize that the cost of operating those roads has tremendously increased. The price of coal has risen to almost three times its former cost; steel has advanced to an equal extent; rails which formerly could be secured for $28, now cost $70; looomotives that formerly cost $20,000, now cost $55,000. You see, therefore, the tremendous operating difficulties those railways had to bear. But

say to them when they start hogging our trade and our ships, " There are men to-day in the Parliament of Canada who do not appreciate your walking off with our business and taking ships that are not necessary." I have been informed that some of our ships which have been taken over by the British authorities for the purpose ol tiansporting munitions and food lay for weeks in the harbours of the United States without cargoes. 'One ship, I understand, lay in New York harbour for six weeks and then had to be taken back again by this Government to its owners., and from the noise that went up there you would have thought there was only one ship left in the Anglo-Saxon fleet, and that we were taking that one over. We must do things in a business-like way. Canada is not a crown colony. We are prepared to pay our way and more than pay our way. We are prepared to finance this war and grow the grain the Allies need in this war and wait for our pay. Where can you get anybody else to do that? That being so, I insist that justice must be done in the allotment of ships, to enable us to carry on our former business, unless it is absolutely impossible.
The ministers of this Government must have a very difficult time. There is always suspicion on account of their political leanings in the past. They are constantly confronted with new problems, and every interest will be trying to pull them in various directions. Members of Parliament on both sides of the House are critical, perhaps a little too much so, but so far as I am concerned, I want it understood that my criticism is made in no carping spirit. In a free Parliament, and a great Parliament such as we have here, it is the duty of every member to speak out and give his views instead of sitting behind and grumbling. The proper thing is to come to the front and say what you want to say. I have endeavoured to keep out of politics and follow the straight path as a Conservative Unionist. But, II am sorry to say that some of the press are trying to make it exceedingly difficult for any member of the great party to which I belong, the Liberal Conservative party, to be a minister of the Union Government in this country. I am referring to the Unionist press. The Conservative party supplies at least sixty-five per cent of the support of this Government.
I was ashamed the other day to see in the Globe newspaper, which professes great friendship for the Unionist party, a mean and contemptible attack on my hon. friend the Minister of Labour (Mr. Crothers) who

happens unfortunately, like myself, to be a Tory. I do not think it is fair. I am ready to take all the blows I get, but when a man is endeavouring to do his duty in a very difficult situation I think that some credit should be given to him and the paper which would be the last to criticise him would be a paper of the opposite party in the Union Government. We want fair play in these things.
The food situation in Canada is critical and the food department of the Government is receiving a tremendous lot of criticism. It is very difficult to decide what to do under the circumstances. But, if the Government is willing to lend an ear to anything I say, and in this I am only voicing the sentiments* of the country, I would favour fixing maximum prices for the principal food commodities so that the poor man will know bow to adjust his breakfast table to the market. Prices have gone far too high. We fixed the price for wheat never expecting that oats and barley would, through some remarkable process, appreciate in value to such an extent as to reach a higher figure than wheat. Give the farmer whatever is the right price for his wheat and adjust the prices also of the other commodities* according to that scale. In Great Britain they have had to come to fixed prices. In this country we are_ paying 37 cents a pound for oleomargarine while in the Old Country the advertised price is 27 cents a pound. The same applies to foods of other kinds such as meal, flour, etc. Why is it that you have to go to the United States to import com in the face of an adverse trade balance in order to meet some requirement of the food controller that we shall not eat white bread? I do not see anything sensible in that. The food controller is collecting taxes under an Order in Council. He is selling a monopoly to a woman who serves a cup of tea in the morning to her boarders; he makes her take out a license. The regulations are so intricate that you cannot tell whether you are breaking the law if you sit down to a meal. Let the regulations be simplified as in the United States. There they have their meatless day and on that day they know they cannot eat meat. Monday is a meatless day and they refrain from eating meat on that day. Tuesday will be a wheatless day and they will not eat any bread that contains wheat on that day. I *am unable to eay whether we have a wheatless day or not. But, I do know that these regulations are yery confusing, that I have

been receiving bunches of correspondence from farmers in my constituency asking such questions as this: " Is it true that I am contravening the law by eating pork or bread on Wednesday?" To my mind, all these confusing regulations are not in keeping with the spirit of the times. I do not offer any criticism of the Pood Controller, excepting that. If Parliament is to give him the right to collect taxes, let it be brought into this House in the form of a Bill and let us put a law on the statute-book. I am -quite willing to vote for it and I do not think a single member will raise an objection, but let us carry on our business- in the proper way. Let us be straight with the people. I do not know but what 1 am going to find an order issued under an 'Order irt 'Council some morning sending me down to Halifax or some place else. I do not say this in criticism. I am only repeating exactly what every man in the country, from one end of it to the other, is saying. Orders in- Council? Why not give us an Order in Council to put 10 per cent on the customs imports and perhaps that would be a reasonable measure. We would get $70,000,000 in that way. That would be an order worth while. In order not to further detain .the House on this particular question, I want to give notice that I intend to discuss the question of Orders in Council the first time we go into Committee of Supply. Ilf nobody else does it I will.
Now, I have offered some criticism to the Government and I trust they- will take it in good part. I trust they will take counsel together in these matters. It is well that the Government has somebody sitting behind it to say some of these things because many people think my way -and if nobody offered criticism against free trade proposals the first thing we would know every factory in this coun.try would be closed. If nobody offered any criticism in regard to railway rates and other matters *concerning the railways the first thing we would know this Parliament House would be occupied by the railways and- we would be all out of business. Somebody has to speak against these things and I think it is the duty of members on this side of the House to express their views just as much as it is that of members of the Opposition and perhaps their word will carry more weight.
I trust that members of this House will take into their consideration that we should do everything we can at this time to stop all this snarling, contemptible agitation and class hatred of various kinds. Do you not think it ie time that we all got together?
Quebec is doing its duty now in so far as the war i-s concerned. There was snarling between Quebec and Ontario, but we know, and everybody knows, that Quebec and Ontario are inevitably husband and wife and they cannot be permanently separated. There is always, however, a nasty hard man who is sticking his nose into our affairs, like Bourassa or LaveTgne, and trying to cause trouble at the fireside. Let us get rid of all these trouble-makers, and let us unite behind this Government to win the war.
They have lost the wedding ring.

They have not lost the
wedding ring. The man who says so says what is untrue, because the ring is not lost. These two peoples must live alongside of each other, and if they are going to live alongside of each other they must have mutual respect for each pther. I can . never lose my respect for the French Canadians. I deplored the situation in Quebec with regard to the war, because I knew what a false position some politicians were putting the men from- Quebec in, virtually branding them as cowards. When, you have a man of French Canadian blood voluntarily interposing his body between you and the enemy, you can never have a hatred of the people of his- race. I very much regret the feelings that have been engendered, but I hope that is all over. I hope we will all look forward to the time after this war is over when- every man who has served his country in the war will he happily employed- in his customary avocation and that we shall see him during his leisure in the evening of his life, -sitting in peace beneath his own vine at 'home enjoying that rest which he has so well earned, -because he has fought for the liberties of the world, and he, more than any one who has not taken part in the struggle, recognizes what the liberty of the world means. We want Canada to be a great country- to be not only a great country from the military standpoint, but great, also, agriculturally and industrially, because we have the motive power necessary to bring that about. We can put power on the belt of our industrial machines at a rate equivalent to coal at $1 a ton, and there is no country in the world where coal will ever again be as low in price as $1 a ton. We are going to be a great farming country, why cannot we be equally as great indus-9 p.m. trially? We are a military nation, why cannot we be also great in a truly national sense? Why can

we not stop this constant stirring up of class hatred, this continuous snarling of one race against the other, and of one business against another, and become a truly united people worthy, in every sense of the term, of those brave men whose blood is to-day being shed so plentifully for our sake, and for the sake of all that we hold most dear in life?
M. D. A. LAFORTUNE (JaoquesdJaritier) (translation): Allow me, Mr. Speaker, to preface the few remarks I am about to make by the last words fallen from the lips of my learned friend who has just taken his seat (Mr. Currie) the hon. gentleman said: "Quebec and Ontario are inevitably husband and wife and they cannot be permanently separated," I am quite willing Sir, to contract marriage with the province of Ontario, but under one condition, namely, that Ontario shall deal justly with me. Husband and wife, forsooth ! After marrying an Englishman, I would not be allowed to apeak. French; that is to say, being his wife, I would be denied the right of speaking my mother-tongue. Or else, I might not be able to speak English, and he might not understand French. How well we would understand one another, at the fireside! How nicely we would live together! He would say: "How dearly I love you, my wife, but take good care you do not speak French.
How isad such a match would be.
It is all very well for the hon. gentleman to make such remarks and say: "Let us live in peace, let us love one another, let us protect one another''; and then, when the question of the French language comes up, to say: "Cut it out, amputate the French tongue, do not speak French in the Ontario Schools, it is a crime." And the hon. gentleman talks about harmony, peace, toleration, "bonne entente". Let him first of all, begin by telling his fellow-countrymen. Let us mete out justice to the province of Quebec; let us .grant the French Canadians full freedom to speak their mother tongue and practice their religion in the province of Ontario." And then we will talk about making love, an dthe courtship may perhaps result in wedlock.
Mr. iSpeaker, it is my honour to represent the mighty county of Jacques Cartier, the most beautiful, the most important, the most wealthy and the most populous in the Dominion.
Since the last election I have moved to Jacques-Cartier as a member of Parliament. I was sorry to leave Montcalm, for the old Administration had given full justice to the voters I had the honour of representing. I

had got from them a great number of public works, a post office, several bridges, good roads, a railway, all sorts of things had been given me by the old Administration which was well-off financially, and as I said I was sorry to leave Montcalm; when that constituency was joined to l'Assomp-tion county, there were two Liberal members, one representing Montcalm-myself- the other representing l'Assomption, my honourable colleague, Mr. Seguin. So I was asked to run in Jacques Cartier the old fortress of the Conservative Party, the old constituency of the ex-Minister of Public Works, the late Honourable F. D Monk. That gentleman represented Jacques Cartier from 1896 to his death, with honour to himself and a little benefit to his constituents. He was a good man, an honost man, a distinguished man, a lawyer of sterling worth.
Since 1878, the year of the famous contests between the late ex-Minister of Justice, Hon. Rodolphe Laflamme and the former M.P., the former Judge of the Supreme Court the late Hon. Desire Girouard, from 1877 up to the death of Mr. Monk the election speeches in Jacques Cartier were always along this line: "You need a bridge from St. Anne to He Perrot and from lie Perrot to Viaudreuil "-they spoke of two bridges. At every election this same appeal was trotted out and the voters were promised; that if the candidate was elected he ;would move heaven tand earth to have both these bridges erected.
Mr Speaker, when I see the millions and millions that are being asked of this House for things which are not indispensable and not a cent in the Estimates for the construction of these bridges, what must I think?
Mr. Monk went through many contests, from 1896 to hi's death, always victorious, always elected with a big majority, and always promising his electors to have these two bridges built.
When he became Minister of Public Works, the people began to feel easier, they began to expect that the bridges would be built, since their representative occupied the most important portfolio in the Government. All in vain; nothing was done. Millions upon millions were voted for all sorts of undertakings, but nary a cent for the St. Anne bridge nor for the lie Perrot bridge.
In a way, I followed the example of my predecessors. I almost promised that these bridges would be built; but if I had known that the Administration we have at present would not include an item in the Estimates for the erection of these bridges, I am not

sure that I would have been willing to run in that county.
If I must face again the voters of Jacques Cartier without these bridges having been constructed, what shall their opinion be of your humble servant? They will certainly point out: " Sir, you are no improvement on our former representatives, who made us the same promises as you did, but who in the like manner failed to make good. You promised us to make every effort and sacrifice, as in the case of the electors of Montcalm, and we blindly believed in your word."
As isoon as this House prorogues, Mr. Speaker, I will begin an electoral tour, and when I will tell my constituents, as I will be forced to, that I failed in having a sufficient amount placed in the Estimates for the erection of these two bridges, what shall they think of me? Being a lawyer, I wi'l endeavour to make the best plea possible, but I can assure you, Sir, that they expect a full account from me, because, as I have already stated, these two bridges must be constructed. How can we conceive that, since the Confederation to this date, when millions and hundreds of millions of dollars have been expended for public works of all kinds, Montreal, the Queen of this Dominion, still remains isolated? How can we imagine that even to-day it is impossible to leave the Island of Montreal by any other means of communication than by row-boat? People are fully served if they can afford to walk, but transportation of this kind is not of a ready use with a heavy load. A light parcel, a suit-case, or other small articles can easily be carried in a row-boat, but transportation becomes impracticable in the case of an automobile; it is better not to take any chance, for it would mean a straight diving to the bottom. The) county o.f Jacques Cartier, as well as Ste. Anne de Bellevue, for years a town, with a great population, having within its limits moist important buildings, such as the Macdonald College, located in the neighbourhood, and for which were freely expended millions over millions of dollars, and which is every year visited by thousands of people from all parts of the country, are nevertheless bereft of means of communication. In order to reach that town, one must cross from Ste. Anne de Bellevue to Vaudreuil, by way of Perrot Island in a row-boat. You may point out that railways are available. Granted. However, the big bug, the powerful, the rich would certainly not be satisfied With it, on account of smoke. Further, we do not enjoy so great a freedom in railway cars, being unable to go back at will.
We cannot travel along in private with beautiful women of our choice, and whose company we crave. In a word, we are somewhat interfered with, whereas in motorcar we leave and return at as early or late an hour as it suits our own convenience, nobody being on the spot to peep or gaze. Well, Mr. Speaker, I state and hold that. these two bridges must necessarily be built from a triple, commercial, intellectual and moral point of view.
lit is with great pleasure and pride that a large hospital is now being erected by the Government at Sainte-Anne \ de Bellevue, and I must especially congratulate the Government who was so well inspired as to construct such an important hospital near the limits of the ICbunty which I have the honour to represent in this House, and this would seem to me an additional reason why honourable ministers1 here present should make all their endeavours to decide and hasten the erection of these bridges. The building of Charlemagne bridge, which , was less necessary, whatever may be said in that connection, was carried out. but it was under the Government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. The Brandon bridge was algo' erected to replace the old one, built years before, .and which was moved twice a year, in the fall, lest it should be crushed by ice, and in the spring at the time of the freshet. Now, if Sir Wilfrid so well succeeded in constructing all these bridges in my former constituency of Montcalm, why should not the present Government be in a position to build the bridges I ask to-day for the county of Jacques-Cartier? Truly, the bridges to which I referred a moment ago were not as costly, but they were needed. Therefore, at the last election, -my opponents were at bay in my electoral district, .and they pointed out: "David is unbeatable". Moreover, Mr. Speaker, I bad the honour of being returned by the voters of Jacques Cartier, as their representative, by a majority of more than 3,200 votes, although a great number of women have cast their votes for my opponent, on account of my getting older. However, I will not quarrel with them for they meant well, and I will endeavour to conquer them at the next election.
The Government friends, who were canvassing in behalf of the Union Government, stated everywhere that the Military Service Act was calculated to protect the farmers' sons, who should never be drafted, and that it was beyond reason to believe that the Union Government, if elected, would enlist the farmers' sons and send them over to

a great many costly works, through the Harbour Commission, to better the lot of the citizens of Montreal.
Now, I tell you, hon. minister, that you have done nothing; there can be no comparison between the necessity for building this tunnel and the very important works you did for Montreal. 1 feel sure that you will grant my request and will see that we get this tunnel and the day it is decided that we will get it I can assure you that it will be a holiday in your honour.
In Lachine, in the beautiful city of La-chine, a plot of land was bought to build a wharf. This land was bought' a long time ago; but the wharf has not been built. In the meantime the people are using the wharf belonging to the Grand Trunk Railway Company and this wharf is in a bad state. If the Government is not ready to build the proposed wharf I would .ask the hon. minister to see to it that the Grand Trunk wharf is repaired while waiting for the Governments. projected wharf to be built. The wharf used ie in bad shape and it would not cost much to repair it so as to make things .a little easier for those whose business forces them to use it.

I am going to repeat in two words what I said a moment ago. It is this: in your division of St. Anne you were elected by a large majority; although you were opposed by a man of sterling worth, of wonderful talent, despite all his efforts you triumphed over him. The people of Ville-Emard, of Monk boulevard, quite numerous, and now that the railway and1 the street cars are coming, now that we are going to have a new line along Cote St. Paul, St. Gabriel, Turcot, Ville-Emard, it is absolutely necessary, hon. minister, now that the tramways are going to run there-the commission has decided to lay new lines in that region- it seems to me, hon. minister that you should put yourself at the head of the movement to give this tunnel to these poor working people so that they will not lose any more time through waiting for the boats to go through and the bridges to be let down.
I have seen 40, 60, 60 and more women and children, poor people, waiting for the bridge to close so they could continue on their

way to work. It is a sorry sight. I feel sure that your sense of justice will not allow this thing to go on .any longer and that you will put yourself, together with your colleague, the Hon. Minister of Marine, at the head1 of our movement and see to it that this tunnel is laid and that these people get fair treatment. I feel confident that you are going to do what I suggest.

Now 1 come hack to the town of Ste. Anne fhait I was speaking of a while ago, to tell this House how badly the town is in need of a post office. It seems to me that this post office is certainly due St. Anne which has quite a population, constantly on the increase; then they have a number of important business establishments, besides Macdonald College, which employs a great many people, and the new naval 'hospital that the Government is now building there. I hope that the Postmaster 'General will think over my request, not forgetting St. Genevieve which is also sorely in need' of a post office. My worthy constituents have asked me to submit their request to the hon. minister; it is my duty to do it; and I do it gladly. During the former 'Government's tenure of office post offices rose as if by enchantment; every city whose population, was sufficiently numerous to warrant a post office being built there was .sure to obtain one from us. I would like to see the present Administration follow the same policy. So, in a nutshell, I say that a post office at both St. Genevieve and Ste. Anne de Bellevue would be very useful.
A moment ago I heard one of the hon. members in the course of the very interest- * ing,remarks he made to the House say that he approved the taxes brought down by the hon. Minister in his budget speech; only he doesn't like the methods used to levy ffiese taxes; he would like to see the people taxed in such a way that they would not notice it. Mr. Speaker, the members who sit in this House are the authorized representatives of the' people and the people have the right to demand that their representatives here be sincere and straight forward. I want to say to the hon. member that when you start out to attain a certain good you should take the best means of getting there and not try to hide the truth. No, Mr. 'Speaker, let us he frank and above board with the people. Let us tell them just how things stand; you cannot, you should not do otherwise. The people who toil and who pay decidedly have the right to demand sincerity in those whom they pay. So I believe that we should speak out frankly to them and tell them the truth about matters. I have never done otherwise.

I remember what our opponents used to say to the old Administration, .about the Quebec bridge; they said that the bridge had fallen down because the Cabinet had *employed incompetent workmen; but they, who claimed to employ for this same bridge the most competent workmen., the greatest experts on the face of the globe, were overtaken by the .same disaster. Yon did not [DOT]see the Liberals take advantage of the opportunity to pass unfair remarks.
.All honour to. those who had a .part in this gigantic undertaking. The bridge is completed.
The Victoria bridge was subsidized'. This bridge had no accommodation for vehicles or pedestrians. It took many millions to alter the bridge so as to accommodate vehicles and pedestrians and help trade on the southern shore. That was done by the Liberal Government.
The Intercolonial. Railway had its terminus at [Levis; the former Government changed this terminus to the Bonavenitune Station at Montreal. The result of this change was astonishing, .and the country will he thankful to Mr. Fielding for it.
We began certain preliminary work on the Georgian Bay Canal. W.e went to considerable expense in this connection, chiefly for excavation and for hydrographic surveys, etc. I regret that this carnal was not continued; the reason given by the old Government was that there were more urgent needs to be met, like the Hudson Bay railroad, the Grand Trunk Pacific and the completion of Montreal harbour. But I hope that before long the country will be in a position to undergo the necessary sacrifices to execute this projet of the Georgian Bay Canal. It would certainly be in the interest of Canadian trade, doing .away with *a distance of some 400 miles .and bringing about .a big reduction in the transportation cost of our western grain.
When the Liberals wanted to change their fiscal policy a little, I think I still hear the hon. gentlemen who were then dn opposition saying: "Don't touch it; let well enough alone", after saying for years that Sir Wilfrid iLaurier was leading the country into bankruptcy; that hie Administration- was worthless. Coming from the Prime Minister and his friends that was quite a compliment to pay the former Administration, If it was a good administration, why did you -oppose it ? Why did you go through the country crying out against waste, .against robbery, and doing your worst to destroy his policy? That is how sincere these gentlemen are..

When the Liberals spoke of building ships in this country they were told that it was a ridiculous idea; and, to hear the Prime Minister of to-day talk then, it was absurd, it was utter nonsense, it was nothing short of childish, to speak of building ship? in our country. Are these gentlemen willing to say the same thing to-day? What hypocrites. They who .are now asking us for millions to build Canadian shine called us ridiculous when Sir Wilfrid Laur.ier .and the Hon. Air. Fielding wanted to do the same thing. That is how sincere they are.
This afternoon an hon. member .said: Give the farmer his Ibushel of wheat. We are not asking you, sir, for our bushel of wheat; we are asking you to leave us the children who belong to us; do not take away the children off our soil; leave these young folk,, the-flower of our people, the future of our country, where they are. You come into our farming districts to -take away the children of 19, 20, 2L and 22 years of age and you talk about increasing agricultural production. Don't you know what is going on in the countryside? We are told:	Take men from the
cities, take women, to work in the fields, Yes, we can take women for ploughing and for harrowing; we will take women for farm work- the -notion is childish! Take men from the- cities, we are told. Yes, they'll come and-work on a farm for a day; but the next morning not one of them will be able to stand on his feet. These things require experience and concentration. I!t isn't, airy Tom, Dick and Harry who can make farming pay. You need practical men; men who have spent their lives on a farm. Those who ladle out this advice to the farmers are off their trolley.
Mr. Speaker, I am through. I know that you will not be sorry, and I am proud that you have given me your kind attention and have listened quietly, as usual, to my remarks. I believed I was keeping within bounds. You did me justice; so much the better; you were decidedly the man to preside over the deliberations of this Chamber and I tender my congratulations to the Prime Minister for having appointed you. He never did .a better thing in hie life. If only he did as well in other resipeets I would be very grateful to him. I thank the House for their kind attention and I resume my . seat, happy if I have been of some use to those who elected me.

Tariff item 27-Coffee, roasted or ground, when not imported direct from the country of growth and production, per pound-British Preferential Tariff 8 cents and 7 i per cent; Intermediate Tariff 10 cents and 10 per cent; General Tariff 10' cents and 10 per cent.
This item calls for both a specific and an ad valorem duty. What is the reason for such a high duty?
We are only increasing the specific duty, not the ad valorem.	.
What is the increase?
The old rate was 4 cents and 74 per cent preferential; the general tariff was 5 cents and 10 per cent.
Will the new rate not be prohibitive?
This item covers indirect importations, on which the tariff is higher than on direct importations for domestic consumption.

Item agreed to.
Tariff item 29a.-Tea n.o.p., per pound-British Preferential Tariff 10 cents and 10 per cent; Intermediate Tariff, 10 cents and 10 per cent; General Tariff, 10 cents and 10 per cent.
What is the difference here?

There always was a tariff on tea under this item, and it had reference to indirect importations. The only difference is that we are adding the ten cents specific duty to the ad valorem duty which was in existence before. The purpose of the duty on indirect importations is to preserve that trade to Canadian business houses, otherwise it would go to the United States or to some other country.
Do you make any distinction in the tea grown in the British possessions?

It is not proposed to give any preference to tea grown in British countries. This tariff is imposed particularly for the purpose of securing revenue, and we are applying here the same principle that we do to importations of liquors and tobaccos. However, there is a great deal to say in favour of granting a preference to British-grown tea

Some years ago, in one of the revisions of the tariff, an item was inserted prohibiting the importation of posters and handbills depicting scenes of crime and violence-I think my recollection of the phraseology is correct. We found that large numbers of printed handbills and posters were being brought in from the United States depicting scenes which could not fail to have an unpleasant effect. I think that item is still in the tariff, and we all agree that it is a wise provision, but I do not suppose that under the wording of the tariff as it stands, that provision would apply to moving picture films. Some of the films which are being brought in today certainly depict scenes of crime and violence and are not of a very elevating character, and I suggest that my hon. friend discuss the matters with the customs officials. Let us make sure that while we prohibit handbills depicting scenes of crime and violence, we do not allow moving pictures to be brought in which are just as bad or worse. It is true that we have censors in each province, but if we use the machinery of the customs to prevent the importation not only of handbills but of

films depicting scenes of 'that character, it would be a step in the right direction.

I do not deny that there is some force in the remarks made by my hon. friend in which he suggests that the excise tax upon cigars be based upon the selling price and not upon the quality. The excise cigar tax in Canada has always been based upon quantity, and I do not feel justified in changing that principle at the present time. In the United Statesfor a number cf years the excise tax upon cigars has been based upon the selling price. If that principle were adopted in the case of a five cent cigar, we would be obliged to apply it to all other excise taxes on cigars. Tire increase in the taxation upon cigars does not exceed two-thirds of a cent for each cigar. In the case of the five cent cigar, it is generally sold to the retail trade .by the manufacturer at $36 per thousand, leaving a profit, selling at five cents, of about forty per cent. This increase in taxation should not at the very most increase the price to the retailer by the manufacturer more than $6 per thousand, or from $36 to $42. Even selling at that price, the retailer would still have a profit of 20 per cent. Again, he could protect himself by adding one cent to the price of a five cent

cigar. It is quite true that in this country the payment of six cents for a cigar is somewhat awkward, but it is not impossible of accomplishment. If, during the present year the increased taxation upon the cheaper cigars, appears to do an injustice to the trade, -at the next session of Parliament we shall give due consideration to the representations that have been made.

medicinal or curative powers or any description as to the amount that constitutes a proper dose; that manufacturers and importers of matches and playing cards be required after the thirtieth day of April, 19*18, to affix to eaon package of matches and playing cards an adhesive stamp of the value of one cent for each one hundred matches or fractional part thereof in a package and of the value of eight cents on each package containing not more than fifty-four playing cards, and that such stamps be placed upon all packages of matches and playing cards held by dealers for sale on the first day of July, 1918, and that such stamps need not be affixed to packages of matches or playing cards manufactured for export; I desire to move an amendment to the resolution. Ae hon. gentlemen will know jewellers carry stocks orver from year to year. That is, a great -many articles ordinarily known as jewellery are not always saleable and have to remain in stock for a long time. The men in the

business represent to me that it will be highly inconvenient tor them to carry jewellery that is taxable and perhaps other jewellery that is not. The wordl "jewellery" is intended to cover only articles for the adornment of the person. I wish to move a further amendment to this resolution, and it is in accordance with the notice which I gave yesterday and which now appears upon the Order Paper, and has reference to the tax upon moving picture films. The amendment is as follows:
Resolved, That at Is expedient to provide that a war excise tax he levied, collected and paid on all cinematograph or moving picture films, positives one and one-eighth of an inch in width and over of fifteen cents on each Aim for each day upon which such film is used.

I draw the attention of the minister to the fact that representations have been made by the smaller moving picture men that the proposed tax is going to put them out of business. It appears to me that, where films are used in very small buildings, where only two or three hundred can be housed at once, these should not be called upon to pay the same rate as houses accommodating two or three thousand. I am not a sponsor for picture shows and rarely attend them, but they are a benefit to many people who desire entertainment at veTy moderate rates, and the soldier, too, frequents these places very largely. I am not offering this by way of any factious criticism at all upon his very estimable way of raising the revenue, but from representations1 which have been made to me it appears that the smaller men will be practically put out of business if some differ-

ence is- not made between the very .small houses and .the very large ones-. This tax, I understand, increases the cost of the ordinary reel from $26 to $50, about 100 per cent of a tax.

My hon. friend was not in the House a few moments ago, when I moved an amendment to the tariff resolution respecting films, reducing the rate from 5 cents a lineal foot to 3 cents, representing a reduction from $50 to $30 upon film reels of one. thousand feet. Having made that reduction, and not wishing to lose any revenue on account of the change, I desire to impose this further tax upon the theatre proprietor, that is, upon those displaying the film. The small theatres use five films per day, as a rule, and the tax would amount to 75 cents per day.

Knowing something about the moving picture business, I think there should be a further change made in the system of placing the tax. In times gone by, the film producers furnished reels of pictures which permitted the small houses to give three different shows each night. The film producers have now changed the size of the reels and made them nearly twice as large, and have increased the price. Consequently the increased size of the reel and greater length of time required to run it takes away one of the shows from, the small picture houses, enabling them to put on only two shows in place of three. The film producers might still further increase the size of the reel and 'if that is done the small houses will have only one show each night. The reduction from 5 cents to 3 cents per foot will help the .small picture shows. I think a picture house should be charged according to the seating capacity. A 500 seating capacity should be charged a certain fee and a show which has 1,000 seating capacity charged a higher rate, and so on. I do not think it is fair to make the tax on a small show equal to that on a large one. The larger houses usually get 30, 35 and 50 cents admission while the small shows get 10 cents in the evening and in the afternoon only 5 cents. This increase in the tax practically puts the small shows out of business. If the Acting Finance Minister would allow this item to stand over I expect a deputation here to wait upon him.
I did not know that this question was coming up to-night or I would have been better prepared.

I am afraid that the size of the theatres changes almost as rapidly as t'he length of the films. However, I may say to my hon. friend that before the Bill which will be founded upon this resolution passes, I shall be pleased to give every consideration to the representations which he has made to-night and which the delegation which is coming shall make.
Does the minister think that the increased cost of films will add anything to the cost of the next Victory Loan?
I hope it did not add anything to the last one.
About $7,000 for films.
I am not aware that it did.
Amendment agreed to.
I have been asked to draw the -attention of the House to the fact that we are now sitting on Ascension Day.
Resolution agreed to.

Resolved, That It is expedient to amend The Business Profits War Tax Act, 1916, and to provide that paragraph (o') of section three be repealed; that any business having a capital of not less than twenty-five thousand dollars and under fifty thousand dollars shall pay a 'tax of twenty-five, per centum of the amount of the profits exceeding ten per cent per annum upon the capital; that the amount paid or payable under the provisions of Part 1 of The Special War Revenue Act, 1915, and The Income War Tax Act, 1917, shall he deducted from the amount payable under the provisions of the above Act, and that in computing the profits of such no taxpayer shall include any tax paid under the said Acts in the expenses of his business ; that the amount of capital in the excepted business mentioned in paragraph (a) of section five of the Business Profits War Tax Act, 1916, be reduced from fifty thousand dollars to twenty-five thousand dollars; that dividends paid during the accounting period shall be considered as a reduction of the unimpaired reserve, rest or accumulated profits; that the provisions of section three of the last mentioned Act be continued in force to the thirty-first day of December, 1918.

The only important amendments contemplated are to provide, first, that the Act shall apply to the accounting period of 1918 and, secondly, that companies employing a capital of $25,000 and up to. $50,000 shall be liable to a business profits tax. The rate applicable to companies employing that amount of capital is that which first prevailed under the Business Profits Tax Act. An exemption of 10 per cent upon the capital em-

ployed is allowed, and 25 per cent of the profits in excess is payable to the Government.
Mr. McM,ASTER: It has been pointed out to me by a business man that in the case of small companies with a capitalization of, say $25,000, operating under a limited liability charter, the profits realized are not so much from the investment of large capital as the reward of the energy and work of the individuals forming the partnership. My correspondent suggested that it was hardly fair to tax a company with so small a capitalization as heavily as the corporations with larger capital are taxed.
The law as it now stands is applicable to partnerships as well as to corporations, though there is a difference in tfie rate.
Practically every resolution that we have dealt with to-night has been amended in some way to make less onerous the burden resting on those who pay taxes, and I urge on the Government t

Many representations have been made to the Government along the lines pointed out by my hon. friend. For the present it is the policy of the Government to renew the business profits tax at the same rate as provided for during the last three accounting periods. It is proposed, however, to- impose this tax only year by year. It is not a tax that might fairly be imposed upon business after the conclusion of the war. The amendment which provides for the re-enacting of clause 3, which is the taxing clause of the Bill, provides that it shall continue in force and be effective only until the 31st day of December, 1918. During that period, the Government will, of course, be glad to hear any representations from the business men of the country, and if it should appear that the tax is too onerous, the Government shall be pleased to give every consideration to such representations. In the meantime, it is the policy of the Government to renew this taxation.

exemption of two hundred dollars be allowed for each dependent child under sixteen years of age; that paragraph (d) of section three be amended, toy striking- out the words "or from the net earnings" ; that subsections one and two of section four be repealed and that it be provided that there shall be assessed, levied and paid upon the income during the preceding year of every person residing or ordinarily resident in Canada or carrying on any business in Canada and upon the income received by any person from any source within Canada the following taxes :-

and in addition thereto,

dollars but not exceeding two hundred thousand dollars;

that corporations and joint stock companies, no matter how created' or organized, shall1 -pay six per centum upon income exceeding three thousand dollars, but shall not be liable to pay the su/pertax; that the minister may permit any corporation or joint stock company the fiscal year of which is not the calendar year, to make a return and to have the tax payable by it computed' upon its income for the twelve months ending with its last fiscal year preceding the date of assessment; that section five be amended by exempting the incomes or such portion of the incomes of judges and retired judges as comes within the provisions of subsection three of section twenty-seven of the Judges Act and the incomes of incorporated companies whose business and assets are carried on and situate entirely outside Canada

Why the exception?
The Judges' Act provides that their salaries shall not be subject to any Federal tax.
That is aij amendment.

No, it is not an amendment; it is simply to carry out the provisions of the Judges' Act. I should like to place upon Hansard a table showing the comparison between our income tax and that of the United States in the case of a married person. It might be of interest to hon. gentlemen.	.
Has the minister a table showing the comparison betweep. what we pay and what the people of Great Britain pay? That might be very illuminating.
It might be very illuminating, but it is a very difficult statement to prepare, apd it would not be as illuminating as a comparison with the income tax in the United States.
If my hon. friend desires it, I shall endeavour to have a statement prepared for him. This is the table of which I have just spoken:

The hon. gentleman has referred to the exemption from taxation of judges. From what classes of taxation are judges exempt? At all events, I suppose that the laws respecting the judges are not like the laws of the Medes and Persians. The judges, above all other things, are just men and I am sure they will not desire to be exempt from any tax, especially in these times, which their poorer neighbours are obliged to pay.

They do not get
salary enough to be taxed.
(Mr. FIELDING:	Lots of us do not get
enough salary, but we have to pay the tax.
I am curious to know from what classes of taxation, the judges are exempt

All salaries or
annuities paid by the Government of Canada to any of the judges are exempt from any tax imposed by the Parliament of Canada. This is only to carry out that provision. Of course, it does not prevent judges .from paying the tax if they so de-. sire. Whether the judges should be exempt or not is a matter of policy. I am not suggesting any change.

How can there be a provision in the law to exempt judges from income tax when we did not have any income tax before last year? Are the judges exempt from customs and excise taxation? We have here a new system of taxation. We are creating an exemption which the judges apparently do not now enjoy. I think the point is worth looking into. The judges are most estimable men, but above everything else they are just, and I am sure they would not desire to he exempted from taxation which their less favoured brethren have to pay. I simply want to protect the judges.

The last clause says:
Corporations and joint stock companies, no matter how created or organized, shall pay six per centum upon income exceeding three thousand dollars hut shall not be liable to pay the -supertax.
Under the Act of last year the income paid by incorporated companies was carried forward to the credit of the shareholders, who. received it later in the form of dividends. Is it the intention to continue that provision? I am not able to ascertain from the wording of the clause whether the income which has been taxed six per cent is to be re-taxed, as though it had paid no tax, after it has been distributed to the shareholder's.

The Act as
amended will only give credit for the normal tax of four per cent. There will he no change.
It says six per cent here.
That is the tax on any income in excess of three thousand dollars. Only the four per cent normal tax paid by corporations will be credited.
Although the corporations pay six?	.
Yes.

Last year the Minister of Finance stated that the sessional indemnity was assessable. I have no objection to that, but the very word "indemnity" suggests, net a salary, but compensation for service which one is called upon to perform for the Crown. Some gentlemen have suggested that in the return to be made the indemnity should be reduced by the amount that has been expended by the member. A member who comes from afar spends a part of his indemnity in Ottawa and he should not be accountable for that in the return.

1 do not desire to detain the House by asking for the information now, but if my hon. friend will make a note of it and 'bring it forward at another stage of the discussion I shall be 'quite content. I cannot see any reason why judges should be exempt. An hon. 'gentleman says that the judges salaries are not big enough. That is true of a great many people. It is a fact that the civil servants all over Canada are very poorly paid. If I may be allowed to say so, having regard to their duties and responsibilities, the most poorly paid officials in the Dominion of Canada are the Ministers of the Crown. They are the only people who have not received an increase in their salaries for the last thirty years. But still they have to pay income tax. I think they escape in the city of Ottawa-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No.
At all events it is quite understood that Ministers of the Crown have to pay this income tax like any other people. If they are to be taxed I cannot see why the judges should be exempt.
I do not wish to be understood as opposing the suggestion of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens, but, as he suggests, the point may he raised later on when the Bill is before the committee.

If judges are exempt it
must be for one of two reasons. The minister said that all judges received their salaries from the Dominion. Government. If the fact of receiving a salary from the Dominion Government is going to be given *as a reason for exemption, I think 'the point raised by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding) is a good one, that it ought to apply to all those who receive a salary from the Dominion Government. (If, it is on account of his judicial capacity, other judges who are not appointed by this 'Government and are not paid by this Government should be exempt. The judge of the general sessions of the peace in Montreal gets his salary from the provincial Government while a judge of the Superior Court gets his salary from the Dominion Government. If, on account of his judicial position, the judge of the Superior 'Court is exempt, why should not the judge of the general sessions atg Montreal, or in any other judicial district, be exempt? On the other hand, if a judge is going to be exempt because the money is paid by the Dominion Government I agree with my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queens that all other people who receive their money from the Dominion Government should be exempt from this tax.

I have the provisions of the Judges Act before me. Section 27, subsection 3 provides: -
The salaries and retiring allowances or annuities shall be pay.able by monthly instalments and shall be free and clear of all taxes and deductions whatsoever imposed' under any Act of the Parliament of Canada.
(Mr. CRONYN: On the consideration of the Bill there will be an opportunity to discuss the point raised by the hon. mem-_ ber for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) as to the increase in the tax in the case of incorporated companies. I do not want to delay the Committee by discussing it, but I think that something might be said on the subject.

Has any further consideration been given to clause 3c of the Business Profits tax, as to a reciprocal arrangement with the United States without which the Business Profits tax that we should receive is paid to them? Has that been taken up?

It is not proposed to submit to the Committee any amendment providing for a reciprocal arrangement with the United States. The Business Profits tax in the United States is based
upon a somewhat different principle from ours. They have ruled that income received by Canadian corporations from products sold in the United States is subject to their Business Profits Tax Act. For instance, our manufacturers of newsprint export to the United States 88 or 89 per cent of their total production. The United States treasury has ruled that the proceeds of sales of newsprint in the United States are subject to taxation under their Act. 'Sir 'Thomas 'White, who ie now in. Washington-, a day or two- ago had an interview with the United -States Treasury Department upon the matter, and, yesterday I had a communication from him assuring me that his representations were sympathetically received by the department and lie thought an understanding would be .reached with respect to the matter.
In other words, there will be no change in the law regarding non-residents?
No. You are referring to the Income Tax Act?
Yes.

I was speaking of the business' profits tax. The matter of reciprocal arrangements- between Canada and other countries, so, as, to avoid a double income tax, was discussed at the Imperial, Conference last year, and I understand 'it was decided to allow it to stand over until after the conclusion of the- war.
Mr. MciMiASTER: I believe that the rate of taxation on incomes over $10,000 is utterly inadequate and I am sure that the country will agree with that view. When this Government is asking the poorer folk to make the sacrifice both in men and money that they are being asked to make, the rate at which the larger incomes are being taxed is utterly inadequate. I know the reply will be given that the United States is taxing incomes on the same ratio. I hardly think that applies. What we want to do is to endeavour to equalize sacrifice as between the citizens of this country, and that is not done by the taxation that if .imposed on the larger incomes.

Is the Acting Minister of Finance aware that a Canadian company with branch factories in the United States doing business there is taxed in the United States upon the profits of these branches and again taxed in Canada upon the same profits it has made in the United States? I know something about this from personal experience. The company is taxed on the

profits of its factories in the United States and when these profits are returned to the parent company in Canada the company is again taxed by the Canadian Government. 1 think it is hardly fair to have to pay such a tax.
Why cannot the minister devise a scheme to avoid this inequality? Because it is a- clear injustice that a man should be compelled to pay a tax in the United States and in Canada.
Do you mean income tax?
Yes, income tax.
I am speaking of the Business Profits Tax.
I am speaking of the income tax.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Business Profits War Tax Resolution was adopted some time ago, and the discussion is now on the Income War Tax Act. It would be more regular, I think, for the hon. gentleman, when we have disposed of this matter, to move to reconsider the one to which he has reference.
I merely draw the attention of the Acting Minister of Finance to this matter so that he may give it consideration.

I would ask the minister whether any action or decision has been arrived at with respect to farming and ranching companies? I want to know whether a farmer w,ho has raised one hundred thousand bushels of grain and sold them for $2 a bushel comes under the Business Profits Tax, and whether a rancher who raises $250,000 on homes and sells them to the Remount Commission comes under the same tax? Has the Government considered whether these industries should be rightly brought under the Business Profits Tax, or left subject only to Income Tax?
I can only say it is not proposed to make these industries liable to the Business Profits Tax.
What justification is there for that?

For the reason that in the cases mentioned, I am told, it is unlikely that the amount of capital employed would he such as to make them liable to the tax, and for other reasons.
IMr. Lalor.]
Are they not businesses just the same as any others that are made subject to the tax?
It was the policy of the Government which introduced this Bill not to make the Acts applicable to them. It would affect only a small class in Canada-
Why shoqld that be a favoured class?

-and the administrative cost would be so' high as to make it not a profitable source of revenue.
Mr. JACOBS. I would like to point out the disparity which, exists between the income tax in Great Britain and that which is proposed to levy under this new Act. I had occasion to look the matter up yesterday, and I find that for the present year the tax is six shillings in the pound on income. That is to say a person with an income of $10,000 would be paying almost one-third of that into the treasury. Now there is a wide difference between paying $392 a year, and paying nearly $3,000 a year on the same income. We have only increased this tax from $380 last year to $392 this year, a difference of $12 per annum. Of course we have started at $2,000 instead of $3,000, but we are only paying $12 more than we paid last year on income. I am talking of an income of $10,000.
It was $360 last year.
We paid $360 last year?
Yes.

But now we are paying on from $2,000 up.
Mr. A. K. .MACLEAN: And $392 will he payable under the Act when amended as proposed.	*
That may be, hut we start from $2,000 instead of $3,000, so we really only have raised the tax $12.
Very well then, $32, but we have started from $2,000.
It does not matter where we have started from.

I am' not imputing motives.
Mr. MoMASTEE: Yes, you are.

I am not imputing motives at all. My hon. friend says that our income tax in Canada is not as large as it is in England. That is a well-known, fact, but there are many reasons why that should be so. In the first place, there is no taxation upon consumption in England, as there is in this country. My hon. friend knows, further, that the customs tax upon practically everything coming into this country is very high indeed. The hon. member for Brome ('Mr. McMaster) very naturally bows assent to that statement, and we are not at variance upon that point. Well, that must be taken into consideration. To suggest that the income tax of Canada should he the same as that of England would, be rather preposterous.

good canon of taxation, well recognized by students and writers, that any new tax should grow gradually, and it should not be at its highest point when the machinery is being formed for its collection. My hon. friend may be quite right in saying that the tax upon an income of $10,000 is too small. It rather has that appearance to me,
I admit. But the- difficulty is, that if you apply a certain rate on the income of $10,000 you must carry that rate right through all the higher incomes, and if you did that the disparity with the United States Income Tax would be very much greater than it is at present. However, I am not arguing that our tax should remain fixed at the present rates forever. Circumstances and conditions in the future may make it absolutely necessary that we increase the present rates. '
iMr. JOSEPH READ: I want to draw the minister's attention to a fallacy he has been making use of with regard to the question of our people going over to the United States if we increase the income tax. If the income tax is increased and money is collected from our people it goes towards paying the debt. If we have a tremendous debt, much larger in proportion than that of the United States, won't our people go into the United States to the same extent by reason of the debt as by reason of the taxes?
I think people in all communities fear taxes more than they fear debt.
I would like to remind the Acting Minister of Finance that by the new time, and by the sun, it is now Ascension Day.
